title: The Absences Haunting the Trump Administration
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
Last week, the White House announced the withdrawal of Lance Schroyer, President Trump’s nominee to direct Immigration and Customs Enforcement

No explanation was offered, though Schroyer, a former Oklahoma state trooper and a confidant of Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, had been criticized for lack of experience in immigration and in leading large organizations
In some ways, a vacancy atop ICE is normal: The agency hasn’t had a Senate-confirmed leader since the day Trump took office in 2017
But the lack of a permanent director is especially notable right now because of the emphasis Trump has put on immigration and the major operations ICE has undertaken during his second term

In the absence of a director, leadership has been split between an acting director, the so-called border czar Tom Homan, the secretary, and the Trump senior adviser Stephen Miller; the administration’s tactics have been volatile , changing often and abruptly
Among many other scandals, ICE agents keep shooting people, some of them American citizens
The department has struggled to recruit and train qualified agents to conduct the mass deportations Trump wants
The vacuum at the top has allowed loose cannons such as the Border Patrol officer Gregory Bovino to (temporarily) seize huge authority
Probably no director could calm all of these problems, but the lack of a Senate-confirmed leader cannot help instill discipline and organization

Trump has stridently attacked what he calls the “deep state,” the corps of permanent civil servants whom the president and some of his aides believe are either layabouts or liberal saboteurs, who, regardless, are determined to bog down his agenda
Using this dubious claim as a basis, the administration has struck serious blows against the civil service
Hundreds of thousands of employees have been fired or pushed out, protections have been eliminated, and there are plans to convert many positions into political appointments

Yet layered above the supposed deep state is what we might call the shallow state: the class of employees who are appointed by each new administration, some subject to Senate confirmation and others not
By intention or negligence, Trump has also left the shallow state riddled with vacancies
The Partnership for Public Service tracks 823 top appointed roles and finds that Trump hasn’t even nominated people for 244 of them
Some of the most notable vacancies are for jobs that would have a central role in implementing Trump’s priorities
The United States is currently sinking deeper into a war with Iran
The president cannot consistently define objectives; no one can explain how or when the war might end, with or without U.S. victory, and the global economy is trembling
But the Defense Department is dealing with this growing crisis with many major jobs open
The department has no secretary of the Army, since Dan Driscoll resigned after feuding with Secretary Pete Hegseth

The Army also has no chief of staff, its top position, after Hegseth forced out General Randy George; senators of both parties are skeptical of Christopher LaNeve, whom Hegseth wants to replace George
Hegseth has ordered a 20 percent reduction in the number of four-star positions, so that allotted positions are left open
The U.S. reportedly faces a serious shortage of munitions, which will take years to fix, but Trump has no assistant secretary for acquisition and no nominee for the role
The rest of the national-security and foreign-policy apparatus is also understaffed

The National Counterterrorism Center, which coordinates federal-government efforts to fight terror, has had no director since Joe Kent resigned in protest of the Iran war (not that Kent, a conspiracy theorist with fringe views, was a wise choice to lead NCTC in the first place)

Despite being embroiled in a war in the Persian Gulf, the U.S. has no ambassadors to the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, or Iraq; it also doesn’t have an ambassador in Yemen, where a rebel group has grabbed some control over another waterway
The U.S. is treating Venezuela as a de facto colony but has no ambassador in Caracas
The president wants to end the war in Ukraine, but he has not sent an ambassador to either Kyiv or Moscow, preferring to rely on the envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, his son-in-law
To be sure, some of the vacancies in the executive branch are a result of Trump’s desire to eliminate or hamstring bodies such as the U.S
Agency for International Development, the Department of Education, and the Federal Election Commission
But plenty of other posts remain unfilled despite their jobs being directly connected to top Trump priorities
Since Todd Blanche was promoted to attorney general, leading the conversion of the Justice Department into a political weapon, Trump has not named a replacement to serve as deputy attorney general
He has proposed major changes to the 2030 census, but the Census Bureau does not have a director
Likewise, he wants to reorganize the National Park Service , but no one has been nominated to lead it

The administration is wrestling with serious water shortages in western reservoirs, but since it withdrew its nominee to head the Bureau of Reclamation, which oversees dams, a year ago, no new commissioner has been named
The Trump administration is, I have written , pushing a kind of big-government conservatism
Trump’s agenda seeks to wield the power of the state more aggressively and intrusively than any other Republican presidency in memory

Some of those efforts have been chillingly effective, but Trump’s undermining of both the shallow and the deep states means that his government struggles to execute even on his most cherished initiatives
That’s bad news for Trump’s agenda, but it might be good news for democracy

title: Egypt’s Warning to Israel
excerpt: W hen Israel’s leaders gathered in Jerusalem on September 26, 2023, to mark the 50th anniversary of the Yom Kippur War, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu descri
body: W hen Israel’s leaders gathered in Jerusalem on September 26, 2023, to mark the 50th anniversary of the Yom Kippur War, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu described the surprise assault by Syria and Egypt as a cautionary tale, one of missed intelligence warnings and self-delusion. “We do not underestimate any threat,” he said
Roughly two hours before Netanyahu took the stage, a chartered Cessna jet linked to Egypt’s intelligence service had touched down at Ben Gurion Airport, about 30 miles away
The jet rolled to a stop in an isolated section of the airport used for sensitive diplomatic and security missions
Abbas Kamel, Egypt’s intelligence chief and one of the region’s most influential security officials, had come to Israel on a most sensitive mission

Hamas, the Muslim Brotherhood–aligned terrorist group that controlled Gaza, appeared to be mobilizing for a major attack, Kamel said, according to Israeli, Egyptian, Arab, U.S., and European officials who were briefed about his visit after October 7
The window to prevent a disaster was closing
He recommended that the Israeli government grant Hamas economic concessions to avert conflict
His message, according to one former Israeli official later briefed on the visit, was: If you don’t change course, Gaza is going to blow up in your faces
Kamel didn’t provide Israeli officials with a date or specific information on what turned out to be a multipronged attack on Israel less than two weeks later, on October 7
And it’s not clear exactly with whom he met

The Egyptian plane remained on the ground in Israel for 67 minutes, according to an Israeli-airport-authority flight log, before returning to Cairo. (Independent flight-tracking applications confirm the plane’s journey.) What the Israeli officials did with Kamel’s warning remains an open question three years after the most devastating surprise attack in Israel’s history
But officials from seven different countries I spoke with said that Kamel’s visit should have set off alarms across the top ranks of the Israeli government
Netanyahu attended a classified briefing following the Yom Kippur War commemoration, according to his public schedule, and soon after approved some economic concessions to Hamas

Officials who spoke with me stressed that the mere presence of the Egyptian intelligence chief in Israel should have demonstrated the urgency of the issue. “The messenger was the message,” a former Israeli official told me. “There is no world,” this official said, where top Israeli officials meet with the head of Egyptian intelligence “and Bibi is not aware.” Netanyahu’s office, in the days after the attack, denied that he’d received any warnings, directly or indirectly, from Egypt over the situation in Gaza
Spokesmen for Netanyahu and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi didn’t respond to my repeated requests for comment when I asked about Kamel’s visit
The then-head of Netanyahu’s national-security council, Tzachi Hanegbi, denied to me this week that there had been a visit from Kamel or an Egyptian warning of any kind

Kamel’s 2023 visit, details of which have not been previously reported, underscores what dozens of sources have told me: that the Israeli government was repeatedly told of threatening activity by Hamas in the lead-up to October 7

A United Nations envoy who was in the Middle East at the time publicly warned of a latent conflict that could bring “grave consequences” while privately scrambling to defuse tensions between Israel and Hamas

The president of the United Arab Emirates, Mohamed bin Zayed, called Netanyahu to warn about the possibility of an imminent attack, after being briefed on intelligence findings from Egyptian and Palestinian sources, according to U.S. and Arab officials with knowledge of the call
Earlier this month, Israel’s Haaretz reported the leaders’ call; I confirmed with multiple officials that the call took place
Netanyahu denied the report and has threatened to sue Haaretz

The UAE didn’t respond to a request for comment. [ Read: Netanyahu just admitted he’s unfit to lead Israel ] Current and former Israeli, Arab, and U.S. officials tell me that they all experienced the same phenomenon in 2023: an arrogance on the part of Netanyahu bred by the deep-seated belief that Israel had the upper hand against Hamas. “It seemed clear that, for whatever reason, the West Bank was their priority,” a former senior U.S. official involved in talks with the Israeli government told me. “They were confident—even cocky—that they had the situation under control.” The Hamas attack, 11 days after Kamel’s visit, resulted in the deaths of approximately 1,200 people, primarily civilians, and the abduction into Gaza of 251 hostages during coordinated raids on communities, military bases, and an outdoor music festival
Israel launched a crushing retaliatory campaign that killed more than 73,000 Palestinians in Gaza, the majority of whom were civilians, according to the territory’s Health Ministry
Hamas’s leadership and thousands of combatants have been killed
The attacks on Israel and the Gaza war that followed produced one of the more devastating humanitarian tragedies of the 21st century
The Netanyahu government’s stunning lack of preparation before the October 7 invasion is perhaps the most important issue in next month’s Israeli election
Netanyahu, who has been prime minister longer than any other politician in Israel’s history, is facing the most serious challenge of his career

Many Israelis, including Netanyahu’s main rival, the former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, have demanded an independent state inquiry into the military and intelligence failures in the run-up to the October 7 attacks
But Netanyahu has continuously refused to set up the kind of independent inquiry that followed past security failures, including the Yom Kippur War
The prime minister has instead attempted to establish a politically appointed commission of inquiry, which he said would include opposition representatives
The attempt was highly controversial; opposition leaders have refused to advance the proposal over concerns that the probe would favor Netanyahu’s government

While the wait for an inquiry continues, dozens of current and former Israeli, Egyptian, Arab, European, and U.S. officials have spoken with me, and their accounts help tell the story of what went wrong that fall
S ince Egypt and Israel signed the Camp David peace accords, in 1978, their relationship can be described as, at best, a cold peace
But the two nations have a common desire to subdue the threat of Hamas and other militant groups in Gaza, which borders both countries
Intelligence sharing between Egypt and Israel has thrived, particularly since al-Sisi became president, in 2014—even when their diplomatic relationship founders

Most of the intelligence reports in the weeks before the October 7 attacks, including Egypt’s, pointed to the renewal of conventional attacks—such as rocket fire—by Hamas and other armed factions in Gaza
They also warned of a spillover of violence into the West Bank

But intelligence sources inside Gaza conveyed to Egypt a more ominous picture, leading Egypt and the UAE to flag to Israel the prospect that something unprecedented was in the works. “For Kamel to go to Israel” for a single hour, an Egyptian official told me about the September 2023 visit, “meant that al-Sisi himself felt: You need to go there and tell them yourself .” The Israeli government’s focus, however, was elsewhere
The country was already in the grip of its deepest domestic crisis in decades

For months, Israel had been consumed by Netanyahu’s effort to overhaul the judicial system, a constitutional confrontation that was protested by hundreds of thousands and opened deep fissures within the military and within society

title: The Show That Always Chased Ratings, No Matter the Cost
excerpt: To Catch a Predator may have presented a simulation of reality, but it was just convincing enough for viewers
body: To Catch a Predator may have presented a simulation of reality, but it was just convincing enough for viewers
The show’s objective was to apprehend people suspected of child sex abuse—which it did by staging sting operations

Its host, Chris Hansen, and his collaborators at Dateline NBC would sparsely furnish the entryway of some rented suburban home; an adult actor posing as a teenager would open the door for a stranger he or she had been chatting with online; and Hansen, who worked as a Dateline correspondent, would lurk in another room, waiting for the right moment to present himself to the houseguest and laconically intervene

His catchphrase was “Have a seat,” which he would utter while inviting his latest subject to take stock of the nightmare unfolding around him: He was suspected of intending to have sex with a minor, Hansen would explain, and now they were on candid camera—the police waiting just outside

Hansen’s somewhat maniacal pursuit of what he considered justice was detailed in last year’s very solid documentary Predators , which explored the legal and ethical limits of To Catch a Predator ’s blockbuster public-shaming approach

The new movie Primetime , a fictionalized look at the host’s meteoric rise and sudden implosion, also has a critical edge, but it’s much more interested in the weird version of real life that Hansen’s show created
The drama, from the director Lance Oppenheim, plunges the viewer into a sordid vision of early-2000s news entertainment—flashy, shallow, flimsy
And it revolves around an energetic Robert Pattinson performance that always feels a little sweaty and desperate to please the audience
Primetime is a beautiful nightmare—and might feel seductive to anyone who wanted to work in the world of gaudy TV journalism in 2004
That’s when the first To Catch a Predator segment premiered on NBC
It was followed by another, in 2005, before airing as a more regular series from 2006 to 2007
When the program ended, it did so amid a legal accusation of wrongdoing (the case was settled) and questions about its ethics
But during the years it ran, popular culture portrayed Hansen as a righteous crusader

His method—ensnaring alleged sex offenders in online traps meant to expose their dark proclivities, before turning them over to law enforcement—made for satisfying TV, mixing the trashiness of Jerry Springer –style talk shows with the aesthetics of supposed hard-news journalism. [ Read: Jerry Springer explained it all ] Casting Pattinson, a true movie star, as Hansen should stack the deck in the character’s favor: He dazzles on-screen
The actor has long been drawn to playing nervy oddities or handsome devils with some insecurity simmering beneath the surface
He portrays Hansen as sharklike and occasionally charming, unable to drop the facade he’s created for his show
He seems to be constantly preening for cameras that aren’t always there
Pattinson’s performance comes across as fake in just the right ways—it’s an impersonation of someone who was himself living as an impersonator
Oppenheim primarily works as a documentarian, and has long been drawn to the anonymous-feeling tract housing and chintzy suburbs that To Catch a Predator made its domain

His documentary Some Kind of Heaven was about a group of retirees living in The Villages, a master-planned neighborhood for senior citizens; Spermworld explored the unregulated online marketplaces for sperm donation, for which people meet in motels to arrange DIY insemination
In Primetime , the director’s first narrative feature, the Dateline crew infiltrate similar types of communities to wreak gleeful havoc in the name of ratings

But the movie doesn’t condemn their efforts so much as it tries to understand how Hansen’s thirst for success infected everyone around him. (The real Hansen has criticized the film, declaring it “detached from reality.”) The most captivating storyline, in fact, is that of a decoy performer

The aspiring Hollywood actor Dan Plumb (played by Skyler Gisondo) takes the gig because he wants a union card, then quickly finds himself dangled in front of suspected sexual predators with little warning

Gisondo’s performance is as sweet and guileless as Pattinson’s is intense and unsettling; Dan has mighty career ambitions, but he sadly fails to grow beyond his seemingly eternal youth and the specific role Hansen has cast him in
Caught between them is the show’s producer Andie (the incredible Merritt Wever), who suppresses any qualms about her professional ethics in search of the show’s next target
Oppenheim imagines the tale of To Catch a Predator as a story of America
This is apt, considering how many stories about this country involve people pursuing success at any cost—one that typically ends up being very high
Primetime eventually careers toward disaster (drawn from the real-life incident that ended the show’s run), but any viewer can see that coming
More fascinating to behold is Hansen’s delight as he gets closer and closer to that grand catastrophe.

title: The Right Way to Adapt a Video Game
excerpt: The moment I knew Resident Evil had me was the ammo check
body: The moment I knew Resident Evil had me was the ammo check

The protagonist of the director Zach Cregger’s new film is a civilian, a medical courier named Bryan (played by Austin Abrams) who’s been tasked with driving a special package over to nearby Raccoon City in the snow

Quickly enough, strange things start to happen: He almost runs over a woman who seems to be sick with a mysterious virus; as the situation disintegrates, he finds himself fending her off with a dead police officer’s pistol
Amidst all the chaos, Bryan slides out his gun’s magazine to count how many bullets he has left
Confirming how many rounds are in the chamber before venturing further into the darkness is a key aspect of the video-game series that Cregger is adapting
But rarely is that ever shown on the big screen
Indeed, the seven Resident Evil films that were made before this one (all but one of which starred Milla Jovovich) took the opposite approach
The characters toted comical varieties of automatic weapons, possessed supernatural abilities, performed amazing vehicular stunts, and pumped thousands of bullets into waves of zombies

The new film’s comparative groundedness is perhaps why Cregger’s initial pitch for a fresh iteration of Resident Evil , one of the best-known video-game properties, resonated with Constantin Films, which holds the rights. “I like the idea of somebody with my skill set and my attitude going into this world,” Cregger told me in an interview of that storytelling choice—that is, turning an unassuming young man whose primary concerns include his girlfriend and his sneakers into a mutant-slaying hero
The director chose not to draw from a specific entry of the game series, which debuted in 1996
Cregger is best known for his first feature film, Barbarian , which announced him as a surprising new talent in the horror world, and for his follow-up, Weapons , which won an Oscar

For his current film, capturing the stressful sensation of actually playing the game was important to him. “ Resident Evil is so simple and so inherently cinematic,” Cregger said, noting that he himself plays it “because the game design and the pacing and the dread is so effective
That, to me, is the heart and soul of those games

It is the feeling you get when you walk into a new environment, and you only have two bullets.” Managing resources, making every shot count, and navigating a world where a monster could jump out from behind any corner—they’re fundamental to the feel of this world, he said
Resident Evil helped create the wildly popular gaming genre known as survival horror, which mixes suspense and action to hook the player
But as with almost any sprawling franchise, it has become burdened by years of continuity
Cregger solves this problem by ignoring most of the backstory for his version

The essential premise is still there: A pharma-bio conglomerate, the Umbrella Corporation, has mistakenly unleashed something called the “T-Virus,” transforming those who are infected into monsters that Bryan must combat in the hopes of survival
The source material usually foregrounds members of law enforcement, most of whom have been featured in past screen adaptations, but Cregger chose to focus on an original character

Bryan fills the role of the average person behind the controller, who’s entered a hostile world barely able to defend himself—forcing him to translate into reality what he’s learned by playing video games. [ Read: A boring video game I can’t put down ] The result is a rollicking, often ridiculous viewing experience, as Bryan hits some lucky shots early on but also makes some rookie mistakes

In one sequence supercharged with video-game logic, he foolishly discards a ladder that could have obviously helped him escape an attic he’s stuck in; in another, he evades a zombie attacker by simply running in circles around an overturned car
As he progresses, Bryan levels up his arsenal, coming across a shotgun and then an automatic weapon

Cregger’s homage to a nasty element of later Resident Evil installments (namely the fourth, which he has called one of his all-time favorite games) is especially amusing: Executing a headshot to kill an enemy can actually be detrimental , as some new tentacled horror might sprout from the neck wound
Bryan’s situation is so absurdly terrifying that laughing as it escalates is inevitable
Humor is, of course, the best way to defuse tension or deflate shocking gore; that’s especially true in moments such as Bryan confronting an infected child or a maternity ward full of mutated babies
Cregger started his career as one of the members of the sketch group the Whitest Kids U’ Know, and his previous movies have a darkly funny edge

He also admitted that the Resident Evil games themselves have “a camp to them that’s undeniable.” Yet Cregger seemed to regret the amount of humor he’d deployed in his take—and that was despite the fact that he’d already pulled some jokes out in the editing process
He had run out the clock, having “turned the movie in at, like, 11:59 p.m. a week before it hit theaters,” he said

Still, he recounted, while watching the finished film, he was thinking, “ I could have lost that; I could have cut that .” He’d also done plenty of big edits, other than just culling lines; the climax, in which Bryan makes it to his destination (a fortified Umbrella lab working on a cure to the virus), in particular changed drastically over time

The scene is filled with comedic actors playing frazzled lab attendants, and initially came across as more outwardly zany. “I had to go and make some really painful cuts to some really great performances and funny, clever things that people were doing in that lab and try and keep it hard-core,” Cregger said

Given the audience’s emotional investment in Bryan’s journey up to that point, however, he realized that they would “not really be in the mood to be chuckling at clever quips that the lab dudes are telling.” To me, though, the humor matches the odd and dissonant tone of some video games, and is thus part of the appeal
The way the film moves through scenes that feel akin to “levels” without feeling schematic was also impressive

Bryan’s first major challenge is at the site of a car crash, after which he trudges to an abandoned house nearby; then he moves through the streets and sewers of Raccoon City, before making it to the lab

Cregger replicates in a way that feels organic the Resident Evil games’ tendency to move players from place to place quickly. [ Read: The Last of Us and the power of video games ] It became obvious how much of a Resident Evil super-fan Cregger is as he referenced detailed aspects of the games that inspired him. (The fairly straightforward path Bryan’s journey takes was another Resident Evil 4 homage, for instance.) Indeed, the entire project came about when he was asked by the film’s producer Roy Lee, who had worked on the Minecraft movie , whether Cregger would ever be interested in adapting a video game. “The only one I could think of would be Resident Evil ,” he said, because he felt that no film had quite yet captured the spirit of playing it

Nevertheless, he faced backlash online from fans for eschewing the franchise’s established characters and plot—a sense of skepticism from a community that often sees their favorite games clunkily translated to the big screen
Cregger was unsurprised. “I was expecting, as D-Day was approaching, I’m gonna get shredded,” he said. “I was already getting shredded by the people who were supposed to like the movie

So, I was just like, well, this is just gonna be the humbling that I am due for.” Instead, the film has been a colossal success for the Resident Evil franchise, earning strong reviews and grossing more in its opening weekend—upwards of $60 million domestically—than any prior adaptation made in its entire U.S. box-office run.Theatergoers, who now comprise multiple generations of video-game fans, have responded to the film’s atmosphere; they’ve never encountered cinema that so closely resembles their side of the player equation

The connection to the source material does matter to Cregger, of course: “The one thing that I really hate is the accusation that I’ve been getting that I just want to make a movie and slap Resident Evil on it,” he said. “This was always supposed to be Resident Evil .” But adapting the franchise doesn’t have to mean engaging with the lore—it can be as simple as capturing a feeling.

title: AI Companies’ New Plan to Keep Themselves From Destroying Everything
excerpt: Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, and Elon Musk don’t agree on much
body: Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, and Elon Musk don’t agree on much

Each started their AI company—Anthropic, OpenAI, and xAI, respectively—out of spite at competitors’ greed and recklessness; each is certain that he alone can be entrusted to build superintelligence safely

But in the midst of the AI panic that has seized the country over the past two weeks, the three CEOs found one point of consensus: the introduction of “embedded evaluators,” or outside experts, to sit inside AI companies and monitor their safety practices
Both Amodei and Altman made express commitments to integrating such evaluations inside their companies
Musk followed with a quote-post stating simply, “Dario is right.” Yet the details of such a system for regulating AI remain vague
How would such a setup work? An unknown number of outside evaluators would be assigned desks to sit at, computers to use, and NDAs to sign
Then, they might seek out risks: Evaluators could spend their days testing whether unreleased models trained for drug discovery can be altered to design viruses too

They might audit organizational practices: Are employees cutting corners on safety in the rush toward the launch of a new model? The evaluators will then write up what they find, and hopefully those reports will see sunlight

Amodei has promised editorial independence, but with significant asterisks: carve-outs for “security-sensitive, legally privileged, commercially sensitive, or third-party confidential information.” Anthropic, OpenAI, and xAI did not immediately respond to requests for comment. [ Read: America’s Hypocritical Take on Intellectual Property ] As for these experts, it seems likely that they’ll come from small nonprofits, as well as large firms

That includes the tech-consulting giant Accenture, with which Anthropic plans to fund a billion-dollar partnership, and the nonprofit METR, which led the investigation of OpenAI agents’ hack of Hugging Face
After that hack, OpenAI granted METR exclusive access to agent transcripts, data sets, and interviews with OpenAI staff
The resulting report revealed concerning levels of cheating and deception among the agents
On-site evaluation has precedent in other high-risk industries such as aviation and banking

The FAA delegates some safety certifications to engineering experts inside airplane manufacturers, whereas the Federal Reserve stations its own supervisors inside banks to enforce regulation. “OpenAI and Anthropic are like Citibank: They pose systemic risk to the globe, so you have examiners,” Brad Carson, a former U.S. representative who is now the president of the AI-governance nonprofit Americans for Responsible Innovation, told me
Yet Amodei’s proposal is still far from a comprehensive AI-auditing regime

As long as safety evaluations remain voluntary, the independent organizations selected by the companies will get as much access as the companies allow to evaluate the specific risks that the companies choose

That doesn’t add up to true independent oversight, and at least some METR employees seem to agree. “None of the work that we’ve done so far passes my bar for an ‘audit’ of an AI company or its systems, and was definitely not ‘regulation’ in any meaningful sense (whether bank examiner–like or otherwise),” Charles Foster, a policy staffer at the organization, wrote on X, speaking in his personal capacity

Recall the Facebook Oversight Board, a legally independent entity created with the ambitious aim to adjudicate the platform’s thorniest speech questions—but which has largely proven powerless to make major decisions that cut against Meta’s interests
Third-party evaluators must walk the line between holding their corporate hosts accountable and not saying anything that gets them booted from the premises
The same access to Slack channels and lunchroom chatter that helps an evaluator conduct whole-organization safety audits can lead to them succumbing to the same blind spots as their host
Here, the 2008 financial crisis offers hard lessons
A Senate investigation found that the New York Fed’s internal culture had been “excessively deferential,” where supervisors feared speaking up about the issues they were supposedly regulating
Moreover, credit-rating agencies were motivated to offer lenient terms to win business from banks

These conflicts of interest are exaggerated when evaluators—like Accenture—are funded directly by the companies. “It doesn’t really seem tolerable to let AI companies pick providers that they have hundreds of millions of dollars of business with to be the primary cops on the beat,” Nathan Calvin, the general counsel of the AI-advocacy group Encode, told me
Then there’s the question of whether the evaluators and the companies they’re asked to monitor are too intertwined
METR, a 43-person organization based in Berkeley, has partnered with the leading AI labs to measure model misalignment since 2023
It does not accept payment or donations from AI companies or employees

Still, many METR staffers come from the same circles as the people they audit, and some have known one another socially and professionally for years. “The AI space is not that large,” Jacob Steinhardt, a Berkeley computer-science professor and the CEO of Transluce, a San Francisco–based AI-evaluation nonprofit, told me. “If you say no former lab employee can ever evaluate any AI model, you are ruling out a pretty broad and important set of expertise.” Those longtime relationships have helped small nonprofits gain access to corporate data, yet they now challenge the organizations’ perceived neutrality. “THESE are the people we’re trusting to beat China in AI? Give me a break,” posted House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, quoting a New York Post cover describing METR employees as “The Woke Wizards of A.I.” Embedded evaluators are surely preferable to the status quo of no oversight at all

The public will learn more about AI incidents when there are watchdogs around—as it has from METR’s Hugging Face report, or Transluce’s recent report on OpenAI agents attempting to hack into a government website

Yet the evaluators will lack teeth and trust until backed by government authority: to license a wide-ranging group of expert organizations, to mandate frontier-AI developers to bring them in, and to set the minimum safety and transparency standards that they must meet. “You need serious oversight,” Gillian Hadfield, a professor of AI governance at Johns Hopkins, told me. “Are we making sure that the entities that are doing this work are qualified? Have we got ways of establishing and maintaining their independence? Do we have a threat that says, ‘If you don’t do this well, you’ll lose your license’?” The worst-case outcome is a race to the bottom: where auditors compete on leniency instead of quality, winning big contracts in return for hasty sign-offs
Meanwhile, it seems that at least some sort of regulation is approaching

In the face of escalating public backlash, internal employee activism, and fears of near-term AI extinction events, both Anthropic and OpenAI have declared support for various forms of state and federal legislation around third-party audits

In a recent podcast , Ben Horowitz—whose venture firm has been a major voice against AI regulation—also seemed to embrace a private-auditor approach, saying that the government “is very good at setting the rules” around unintended model behaviors, whereas “a very competent private company” should evaluate compliance
The Overton window in Silicon Valley is shifting
But if the stakes really are existential, hiring a few extra inspectors falls painfully short—especially when the details of the arrangements are this slippery
Some politicians, facing an angry and frightened public, have turned to more aggressive asks, such as nuclear-style treaties with China and a ban on superintelligence itself

Two years ago, California Governor Gavin Newsom vetoed a state bill that included mandated third-party audits, among other safety requirements, after a fierce lobbying campaign by OpenAI and Andreessen Horowitz. (Anthropic was an exception, expressing conditional support.) Last week, Newsom—sensing the changing tides—issued an executive order to require onsite auditors and accelerate the development of an “AI kill switch.” President Trump still has his foot on the gas pedal. “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT,” he posted last week
In June, the administration told CAISI, the federal government’s internal AI-evaluation unit, to stop publishing its reports
Trump’s accelerationism—informed by his rapport with ballroom sponsor and NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang—likely dooms federal AI-safety regulation for now
It’s nice to see some AI-industry leaders agreeing that someone else should rein them in

title: The Two-Year Temper Tantrum to Come
excerpt: Yesterday when a judge ordered President Trump to lift a ban on journalists accessing the White House, the immediate crisis appeared to be averted: Trump had lo
body: Yesterday when a judge ordered President Trump to lift a ban on journalists accessing the White House, the immediate crisis appeared to be averted: Trump had lost, and reporters from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico largely returned to their normal work on the grounds
But the maneuver Trump had attempted is a preview of what to expect over Trump’s remaining time in office—especially if Democrats take control of one or both chambers of Congress
To put it another way, the country is headed toward a two-year temper tantrum

Last Friday, Trump announced on Truth Social that he would ban journalists from the three outlets from the White House “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” The reporters promptly sued; in the meantime, the television networks responsible for White House pool coverage suspended that work
The counterproductive result was an odd several days during which Trump went without the traditional passel of reporters hanging on his every word
On Monday, at the unveiling of a new White House helipad, Trump’s remarks were inaudible without the powerful boom microphones used by TV crews
Video streamed by administration staffers showed the vaguely comic sight of Trump silently gesticulating, his mouth moving but no sound coming out
The whole kerfuffle was a display of both Trump’s power and his impotence: damaging to democracy yet also undermining of his own authority
What prompted this particular round of White House abuse of the press is not entirely clear

But Trump often resorts to attacking the media when he receives news he dislikes—and amid rising fuel prices caused by the war in Iran, sinking poll numbers for the congressional GOP, and Trump’s own declining popularity, there is a lot of bad news for the president to avoid

So he created a safe space. “I don’t have to let them into my—into the people’s house,” he declared from the Oval Office of journalists writing “purposely negative stories.” During that same exchange with reporters, Trump was asked whether he thought the ban would survive a court challenge

He didn’t seem to care: “I think it’s good to point it out, whether it survives or doesn’t.” Timothy Kelly, the Trump-appointed judge assigned to the case filed by CNN, MS NOW, and Politico , had previously ruled in 2018 that the White House could not bar CNN’s Jim Acosta
Kelly was now also armed with a 2020 ruling by the U.S
Circuit that journalists granted access to the president could not be stripped of it without due process

By banning the three outlets, Trump had chosen to pick a fight that he had already lost twice in court and would almost certainly lose again. [ Matt Viser: Trump’s public service announcement: ‘Love me’ ] The Department of Justice’s litigating approach this time around proved haphazard

Perhaps seeking to exploit the courts’ traditional reluctance to interfere on national-security issues, DOJ invoked those magic words as a justification, saying that the outlets had supposedly used their White House access to obtain leaks dangerous to the country’s security

But one of the ostensible leaks published by Politico turned out to have been a quote provided during an authorized White House press call by an administration official—Vice President Vance himself, according to the media reporter Oliver Darcy
The whole exercise was a tidy summary of the Justice Department’s transformation into an extension of Trump’s id
At one point, hours after a court hearing, the DOJ lawyer leading the case, Michael Velchik, submitted a legal filing that consisted primarily of a brand-new Truth Social post from the president

The argument that national security required the revocation of press access “lacks factual support,” he wrote in an emergency ruling early yesterday morning, ordering the White House to allow the journalists back in
When the press arrived at the White House gates hours later, however, the reporters from the three disfavored outlets were still barred from entering

What appeared at first to be Trump’s defiance of a court order may instead be attributable simply to incompetence, thanks to delay and confusion on the White House and Secret Service’s end in implementing Kelly’s directive
Either way, the TV press pool refused to resume operations until this morning
The result was that Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s state visit to the White House yesterday took place without any American live television coverage

Trump also barred some—though, confusingly, not all—CNN and MS NOW journalists from covering the state dinner, which does not directly violate Kelly’s order but could land the White House back in the courtroom
There is no strategy here: The only real result of his fit of pique has been to deprive himself of the attention he covets
Meanwhile, he managed to inspire media organizations to join together in solidarity—depriving him of pool coverage

Even the Trump-friendly Fox News joined an amicus brief filed by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press against the ban. ( The Atlantic joined the brief as well.) [ Olga Khazan: A revealing exchange between Donald Trump and Kaitlan Collins ] Trump’s standoff with the press reflects the fury of a man who has grasped, however dimly, that he cannot control everything. (“You should not be here covering me,” he told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins at the United Nations General Assembly meeting in New York earlier this week, seemingly not understanding that banning CNN from the White House did not mean the network would be universally banned from his presence.) It is also the fury of someone insistent on exerting as much power as he can over the steadily shrinking universe of what does remain directly under his control
If Republicans lose unified control of Congress in the midterms, then Trump’s old allies will be less likely to swear fealty, and that universe will diminish even further
There is a danger to democracy here, but it is less the danger of a strategic shift toward authoritarianism and more the danger of petulance and stupidity
Every president struggles with irrelevance in the waning years of their power, and Trump has never been one to decline gracefully.

title: The Download: the Pentagon’s AI-powered lie detector and young organ limits

body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology

The Pentagon wants $30 million to build an AI-powered lie detector The US government wants to spend $30.3 million over the next five years on an improved lie detector, according to a Department of Defense budget request

The program, called “Polygraph+” or “Polygraph Next,” will focus on scoring algorithms that use AI and machine learning, as well as a technique called “standoff sensing,” which can take physiological readings from a person without attaching a device to them
The project aims to improve the accuracy and reliability of polygraph assessments
But it could just be the latest in a long line of failed attempts to use technology to detect lies

Here’s how the program could work—and why experts say AI-enabled lie detection is “the worst of both worlds.” —Amit Katwala Young organs may not be a fountain of youth for recipients Around this time last year, a hot mic caught Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping discussing the possibility of living forever . “With the developments of biotechnology, human organs can be continuously transplanted, and people can live younger and younger, and even achieve immortality,” Putin reportedly said
He seemed to be referring to the “replacement” theory of longevity, supported by experiments that involved physically stitching young mice to old ones
Unfortunately for Putin, new research on transplanted hearts pours a little cold water on this idea
But it also offers useful insights for organ transplantation
Find out what the research reveals about the limits of rejuvenation . —Jessica Hamzelou This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter

title: The Pentagon wants $30 million to build an AI-powered lie detector
excerpt: The Pentagon wants a smarter lie detector: The Department of Defense is requesting $30.3 million over five years for "Polygraph+"—an AI-powered upgrade to tradi
body: The Pentagon wants a smarter lie detector: The Department of Defense is requesting $30.3 million over five years for "Polygraph+"—an AI-powered upgrade to traditional polygraph technology that could read physiological signals without touching the subject

The science still doesn't hold up: Polygraph technology has been repeatedly debunked since its invention in the 1920s, with a landmark government report calling the evidence for its accuracy "weak at best"—and experts warn AI adds uncertainty on top of an already invalid tool

There's no universal tell for lying: Researchers say the fundamental problem remains unsolved: There is no single physiological signal that reliably indicates deception in all people, making any technology built on that premise structurally flawed

Critics see intimidation, not investigation: Legal scholars warn that the real purpose may be less about catching liars and more about pressuring people to confess—particularly as the Pentagon ramps up polygraph use to hunt for press leakers under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. " data-chronoton-post-id="1145144" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> The US government wants to spend $30.3 million over the next five years on an improved form of lie detector, according to a Department of Defense budget request

The program, called Polygraph+ or Polygraph Next, will focus on scoring algorithms that use artificial intelligence and machine learning and on a technique called “standoff sensing,” which refers to the ability to take physiological readings without attaching a device to a subject’s person

According to details of the budget document, which were first reported by Inside Defense , the project will “modernize federal polygraph and credibility assessment technologies” to improve their accuracy and reliability

But the project may be just the latest in a long line of failed attempts to use technology to detect lies. “It’s a misguided effort to reduce the complex to something that is tangible,” says Kyri Kotsoglou, a legal scholar at Northumbria University in the UK who studies the use of polygraphs in the justice system
The move comes at a time of high tension within the department
Under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the Pentagon has been increasingly turning to polygraph tests in an attempt to find the sources of alleged leaks to the press

In September, the New York Times reported that around 50 officers on the Joint Staff had been given polygraph tests after news coverage reported on the depletion of US weapons stockpiles in the war with Iran.  Polygraph+ will be run by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA), which conducts background checks for the federal government

According to the budget document, which has not yet been approved by Congress, the new technology will be used for vetting of prospective employees and “insider threat detection.” It is not yet clear which specific technologies will be used, and the DCSA did not respond to a request for more information.  But other Pentagon efforts offer potential clues
In 2023, the department’s Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) ran an open submission process to find companies with products that could be used for deception detection

It selected two companies to build prototypes : Presage Technologies, which claims to be able to measure heart rate and breathing rate using standard cameras, and Altec Research, a medical sensor company now branching out into non-contact sensing technologies
A screenshot of Altec’s prototype technology released by the DIU shows that it tracks head movement, facial skin temperature, and pore activity
Presage Technologies and Altec Research did not respond to requests for comment
The DIU declined to comment.  Altec Research has built a prototype that tracks head movement, facial skin temperature, and pore activity
ALTEC RESEARCH Current lie detection technology has barely changed since the polygraph was invented in the 1920s
Examiners rely on blood pressure, pulse, breathing, and sweat measurements to determine if someone is lying

They make judgments about the veracity of respondents’ replies on the basis of differences in their physiological response to baseline questions like “Is the sky blue?” and target questions like “Have you ever committed a crime?” The federal government conducts tens of thousands of the tests each year while screening employees, but the reliability of this technology has been repeatedly challenged—and its results are rarely admissible in court

In 1983, Congress’s Office of Technology Assessment concluded that there was very limited evidence supporting the polygraph’s use for screening employees, and in 2003 , the US National Research Council (NRC) said evidence for its efficacy was “weak at best.”  Research suggests humans can spot a lie just over half the time without any technical assistance
The American Polygraph Association claims the polygraph is between 80% and 94% accurate
But the 2003 NRC report pointed out that a screening test with this level of accuracy could still lead to a lot of mistakes
The DOD employs 2.8 million people; an imperfect system applied at that scale could end up falsely accusing tens of thousands
Polygraph interpretations are often subjective: Different examiners get wildly different results , and people from minority groups are more likely to be judged as deceptive

What’s more, with training it’s possible for interviewees to learn a variety of countermeasures that can help beat the test; for example, they may artificially heighten their physiological response to baseline questions by stepping on a pin hidden in their shoe.  “If you know how it works, you can beat it,” says Sophie van der Zee, an associate professor who studies deception at Erasmus University in Rotterdam
She says the machine’s biggest effect is deterrence—often, subjects confess before it even begins. “But that only works if people think a polygraph works,” she points out
Various new strategies for lie detection have been attempted over the decades , with technologies ranging from thermal cameras to pupil trackers to brain scans
None of them have yielded reliable results outside the lab

The problem is that there’s no single telltale sign of lying that’s true for everyone all the time. “There is still no Pinocchio’s nose,” says van der Zee.  AI could theoretically improve polygraphs if it could find patterns in the data that examiners can’t
AI algorithms are also more likely to be used for “multi-modal” deception detection, which seeks to combine multiple measurements into an overall deception “score” that is harder for people to game

Three things are happening under the surface that lie detection tries to home in on, van der Zee says: physiological stress, cognitive load, and the conscious efforts people make to conceal the fact that they’re lying
Current polygraph technology tackles only one. “The more you can have combined methods that approach it from these three different angles, the more successful you will be,” van der Zee says
This isn’t a new concept—in the 2000s, researchers at Manchester Metropolitan University in the UK developed a system called Silent Talker that generated a deception score from video footage
This was later folded into iBorderCtrl, an EU-funded pilot program
In the US, a project called AVATAR incorporated eye tracking, voice analysis, and body movement detection into a tool for use at border crossings
All these projects have quietly faded away.  Kotsoglou says combining AI and the polygraph is “the worst of both worlds” because it adds uncertainty on top of invalidity

Even if AI or machine learning can spot previously unseen patterns in physiological data, it won’t be able to reliably link them to lying because there is no real ground truth.  “Even if you have all the records in the world from polygraph tests, you don’t know whether those polygraph tests are right or not,” says Marion Oswald, a professor of law who has written with Kotsoglou on the use of polygraphs in the justice system

She fears that new forms of lie detection will, like the polygraph, be used more as a psychological prop than a scientific tool.  “It seems very much a response to the concern of the current administration to leaks and perceived lack of loyalty,” says Oswald. “[Lie detection is] being used as a threat, to intimidate and force people to confess to things, as opposed to anything that’s actually getting valid information.”

title: Young organs may not be a fountain of youth for recipients
excerpt: Young hearts don't stay young for long: New research shows that transplanted hearts quickly take on the biological age of whoever receives them — meaning a
body: Young hearts don't stay young for long: New research shows that transplanted hearts quickly take on the biological age of whoever receives them — meaning a 30-year-old heart given to a 70-year-old recipient will soon "act" 70

The body's environment calls the shots: Researchers found that neither the recipient's blood nor other organs were meaningfully affected by the donor heart's age, suggesting the body's broader environment overpowers any rejuvenating potential a young organ might carry

A silver lining for transplant medicine: The findings could push surgeons to stop discarding older donor hearts, since biological age appears to reset after transplant anyway — potentially expanding a critically short supply of viable organs

Immortality remains out of reach: The study underscores just how stubbornly complex aging is — reversing it entirely would require unwinding DNA damage, structural decay, and cellular wear across every tissue simultaneously, which scientists say is an enormous, likely impossible, challenge. " data-chronoton-post-id="1145083" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Around this time last year I was attending an aging conference in Manchester, listening to a talk about fly aging, when my phone started pinging

News outlets were reporting that a hot mic had caught Russia’s and China’s leaders discussing the possibility of living forever . “With the developments of biotechnology, human organs can be continuously transplanted, and people can live younger and younger, and even achieve immortality,” Russia’s Vladimir Putin reportedly told China’s Xi Jinping
He seems to have been referring to the “replacement” theory of longevity, which has been supported by multiple experiments that involved physically stitching young mice to old ones
Something about the young blood rejuvenated the old mice
Perhaps young organs could rejuvenate world leaders in their 70s, too
Unfortunately for Putin, new research pours a little cold water on this idea
Studies on transplanted hearts in both mice and humans suggest that new hearts soon adopt the biological age of the recipient, no matter how young they were to begin with
The finding could be important for transplantation, but it also highlights just how complex aging—and rejuvenation—are
Jesse Poganik at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston is one of the many scientists trying to understand exactly what it is about the bodies of young mice that rejuvenates old ones
Plenty of research has focused on seeking the secrets of youth in young blood
But what if it’s something about young organs instead? To find out, he and his colleagues performed a set of heart transplants in mice

In humans, heart transplants typically involve removing a damaged or injured heart and replacing it with another from a donor who is usually much younger than the recipient. (When Poganik assessed hospital records, he found that most recipients were about 20 years older than their donors.) The mouse transplants were different: Mice received a second heart, implanted in the neck—a procedure that’s slightly simpler and allows scientists to compare the new hearts with the existing ones
In some cases, young adult mice were given a heart from a middle-aged donor
In others, middle-aged mice got young hearts
The team used a trio of “aging clocks” —molecular tools used to estimate the biological ages of tissues and whole organisms—to assess whether the additional hearts affected the mice in any way
These clocks were good at predicting the chronological age of mice that didn’t get new hearts
Poganik says he was expecting to see a reciprocal effect, and that young hearts might benefit older animals, for example
In previous work by other members of his team, young mice that got old hearts experienced a buildup of senescent cells in their other organs
These cells are thought to contribute to the aging process, suggesting that receiving an old organ might prematurely age an animal
When he and his colleagues analyzed the transplanted hearts between four and six months after surgery, they found that the hearts seemed to have adopted the biological age of the recipients
Young hearts got older, and old hearts got younger. “The environment of the transplanted organ really dictates how it seems to behave biologically,” he says
The findings were published online at bioRxiv last week

The team also looked at each mouse’s blood and other organs—including its original heart—and were surprised to find that they seemed to be unaffected by the presence of the new heart, despite the age of its donor
The finding was backed up by data from human heart transplants
People who receive a donor heart must typically undergo a series of heart biopsies after surgery
The tiny pieces of heart tissue collected from people who had heart transplants at Brigham and Women’s have been stored for decades

And when Poganik and his colleagues tested their biological ages with the aging clocks, they found a similar pattern: No matter the age of the donor, a new heart quickly adopts the biological age of the person who received it

It’s not clear why this is, but João Pedro de Magalhães, who studies aging at the University of Birmingham in the UK and was not involved in the study, thinks it might have something to do with the recipient’s immune system
Perhaps immune cells circulating in the blood might affect markers of aging in the new organ, he says
Perhaps the potential rejuvenating effects of a young heart end up being diluted by all the other aged components of an older body, Poganik suggests
Or maybe a single organ just isn’t enough to see an effect

Poganik hopes his finding will encourage surgeons to consider using hearts from older donors, many of which are discarded on the assumption they won’t function as well. (Machines used to preserve organs before transplantation are changing that already—and Poganik has worked on another study showing that these devices seem to rejuvenate donor livers to some extent.) But the study also highlights just how complicated aging is

If organs seem to be getting older by one measure but not by another, how can we get a full picture of the biological age of an organ, or a person? This complexity means that scientists are not likely to discover a true way to completely reverse aging, says Poganik. “That would mean that every aspect of aging has to go back in time,” he says

Reversing DNA damage, structural damage, and all the other degradations that are part of the aging package, across all our various cells and tissues, presents an enormous challenge. “There are aspects of biological age that are probably reversible, and there are aspects that are probably not,” he says

title: In ‘NAZA,’ Israeli whistleblowers’ revelations about civilian deaths in Gaza reflect a longer history of Palestinian isolation

<title>In ‘NAZA,’ Israeli whistleblowers’ revelations about civilian deaths in Gaza reflect a longer history of Palestinian isolation</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762096/original/file-20260924-60-i55q85.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C8256%2C5504&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">&#39;NAZA&#39; filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor conducted interviews with anonymous members of Israeli military and intelligence services from the rooftops of Tel Aviv, Israel.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/general-view-shows-the-israeli-city-of-tel-aviv-on-august-news-photo/2165972971?adppopup=true">Gil Cohen-Magen/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>There’s a powerful scene in Moroccan-French-Israeli filmmaker Simone Bitton’s 2004 documentary “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0413018/">Wall</a>,” which tells the story of the construction of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/08865655.2016.1174601">the West Bank barrier</a>, a 448-mile – or 721-kilometer – network of walls and fences dividing large parts of the West Bank from Israel.</p>

<p>A concrete slab is slowly lowered into place in order to complete a section of the wall. Inch by inch, the vibrant, hilly Palestinian community on the other side gets smaller and smaller. </p>

<p>And then – just like that – a world that’s a stone’s throw away is gone. </p>

<p><a href="https://edinburghuniversitypress.com/book-israel-palestine.html">As someone</a> <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/arrested-movement-in-the-middle-east-9780755656721/">who studies</a> the restrictions placed on Palestinians, I often think about this scene as a microcosm of Israel’s decades-long use of walls, checkpoints and surveillance technologies to seal off Palestinians from the rest of society.</p>

<p>Nowhere is this dynamic more evident than the Gaza Strip, which Israel <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/45406228">fenced in during the 1990s</a> and has <a href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2214163">blockaded since 2007</a>, citing security concerns and the threat of militant attacks.</p>

<p>Thanks to these barriers, the immense suffering of Palestinians in Gaza – <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cvgpd1x00exo">more than 70,000</a> of whom have been killed as a result of the Israel-Hamas war since 2023 – has been difficult to document. The Israeli government largely bars international journalists from entering the Gaza Strip independently, while Palestinians in Gaza are generally not allowed to leave the Gaza Strip.</p>

<p>But the Sept. 10, 2026, premiere of Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s film “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt44766123/">NAZA</a>” at the Venice International Film Festival has put the spotlight on the ongoing tragedy in Gaza without relying on footage of gruesome corpses or bombed-out neighborhoods. </p>

<p>The film consists largely of anonymous testimony from 24 members of Israel’s military and intelligence services. They discuss the ways in which <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/sep/11/naza-directors-film-israeli-intelligence-rachel-szor-yuval-abraham-">Israel has used artificial intelligence</a> to target Hamas officials, despite knowing the attacks will also generate large numbers of civilian casualties. The title, “NAZA,” comes from an acronym for the Hebrew phrase “nezek agavi,” or “collateral damage,” and it’s the Israeli military’s threshold system for how many civilian casualties are acceptable in its military strikes on Gaza since <a href="https://www.cfr.org/global-conflict-tracker/conflict/israeli-palestinian-conflict">the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks</a>. Hamas-led militants from Gaza launched those attacks in southern Israel, murdering 1,200 people – mostly civilians – and also taking about 250 hostages.</p>

<p>To me, part of the film’s power lies in its focus on the clinical way of carrying out strikes on Gaza from a distance. But the Israeli military’s approach could only work after systematically isolating the Palestinian people over the course of decades.</p>

<h2>Unseen victims</h2>

<p>In addition to constructing walls and blockading Gaza, Israel has enforced separation of Palestinians <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/14650045.2011.562944">by restricting or denying permits</a> to Palestinians wishing to enter or work in Israel through <a href="https://www.versobooks.com/products/2007-hollow-land">aerial surveillance</a> and <a href="https://www.versobooks.com/products/2007-hollow-land">through the expansion</a> of Israeli settlements in the West Bank.  </p>

<p>Both the visual language and the content of “NAZA” reflect and reveal how knowledge of Palestinian suffering is often mitigated in Israeli culture, politics and daily life. </p>

<p>The film juxtaposes audio of Israeli soldiers’ testimony with shots of the Tel Aviv cityscape at night. In these interviews, the soldiers map out how targets are chosen, how attacks are planned and how much leeway is given for civilian casualties. </p>

<p>The victims themselves are largely unseen, despite their close proximity: Tel Aviv sits a mere 43 miles – or 70 kilometers – up the coast from the Gaza Strip. </p>

<p>The choice to film primarily at night, in darkness, using disembodied voices to tell a story not depicted on camera, further highlights the extent to which these events have been obscured in Israel and around the world. Perhaps that’s why the Israeli government has gone to such great lengths to discredit the film, saying it contains “<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/sep/14/gaza-documentary-makers-naza-israel-citizenship-ntwnfb?">deliberate distortions of reality</a>.” Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/14/world/middleeast/israel-naza-documentary-backlash.html">has threatened to revoke the citizenship of its directors</a>. </p>

<p>In response to the interest and backlash surrounding the film, <a href="https://x.com/yuval_abraham/status/2103061893913162054">the filmmakers announced</a> that “NAZA” will be available to stream for free, for anyone to see, beginning in November 2026.</p>

<h2>Breaking through</h2>

<p>“NAZA” highlights a psychological distance between attacker and attacked that was enabled by AI, computer screens and the physical isolation of the targets. Yet it is far from the first film to call attention to the invisibility of Palestinians.</p>

<p>Elia Suleiman’s 2002 dark comedy “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0274428/">Divine Intervention</a>” repeatedly stages scenes in which Palestinian characters are stuck at or try to get around an Israeli military checkpoint. And Yoav Shamir’s 2003 documentary “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0391857/">Checkpoint</a>” chronicles everyday interactions between Palestinians and Israeli soldiers at checkpoints in the West Bank and Gaza. </p>

<p>Other films center on acts of transgression or protest. Hany Abu-Assad’s 2013 drama “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt2852406/">Omar</a>” and Ameen Nayfeh’s 2020 drama “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt12246266/">200 Meters</a>” both feature Palestinian characters who break the law and surreptitiously cross the West Bank border into Israeli territory, exposing themselves to physical and legal danger.</p>

<p>“<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt30953759/">No Other Land</a>” – the 2024 documentary <a href="https://theconversation.com/a-palestinian-israeli-film-just-won-an-oscar-so-why-is-it-so-hard-to-see-249233">that netted Abraham and Szor an Oscar</a>, along with fellow directors Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal – points the camera on Palestinian protest movements against land expropriations and home demolitions in the West Bank. In the 2011 film “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt2125423/">5 Broken Cameras</a>,” Palestinian farmer Emad Burnat captures his West Bank village’s struggle against the construction of a massive wall that chokes off farmland and access to vital resources. Even as his cameras are repeatedly damaged or destroyed, Burnat refuses to stop documenting the resistance.</p>

            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/40KW6knYMo4?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">‘NAZA’ will be available to stream for free starting in November 2026.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Crying while shooting</h2>

<p>“NAZA” also points to another phenomenon: how isolation and separation encourage complicity. The physical distance between Israeli soldiers and the people they target may make it easier to go along with or ignore what is happening.</p>

<p>In this way, “NAZA” grapples with a trope in Israeli films and literature of exploring the guilt of Israeli soldiers. Sometimes derisively referred to by critics as “<a href="https://academic.oup.com/screen/article-abstract/54/1/44/1623426">shooting and crying</a>,” the thematic framework of these films has been criticized for focusing on Israeli moral anguish at the expense of Palestinian experiences and perspectives.</p>

<p>For example, S. Yizhar’s 1949 novel, “Khirbet Khizeh,” which was adapted <a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0151202/">into a film</a> in 1978, tells the story from the perspective of Micha, an Israeli soldier fighting in the 1948 war that established the state of Israel. He’s part of a squad that expels Palestinians from their village, and his ensuing guilt provokes a crisis of conscience that haunts him for years to come. </p>

<p>Decades later, the 2008 animated documentary “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1185616/">Waltz With Bashir</a>” follows the film’s director, Ari Folman, as he plumbs his repressed memories of his participation in the <a href="https://www.npr.org/2007/08/28/12744311/timeline-1982-siege-of-beirut">1982 Israeli invasion of Beirut</a> and how he inadvertently helped Lebanese Christian Phalangist militia fighters carry out <a href="https://imeu.org/resources/resources/explainer-the-sabra-shatila-massacre/113">massacres of Palestinians at the Sabra and Shatila refugee camps</a>.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/uWo8U5J0XeY?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">‘Waltz With Bashir’ centered on the fragmented memories, trauma and guilt of an Israeli soldier who had helped facilitate the Sabra and Shatila massacre in Beirut, Lebanon, in 1982.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The “shooting and crying” genre was largely accepted in mainstream Israeli culture, with “Khirbet Khizeh” <a href="https://muse.jhu.edu/pub/1/article/963600/summary">taught in Israeli schools</a> for decades. But the Israeli government’s hostile reaction to “NAZA” perhaps signals not only the growing intolerance of dissent in Israel, but also a <a href="https://contendingmodernities.nd.edu/global-currents/shooting-and-singing/">fading cultural and political concern</a> with the morality of Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territory.</p>

<h2>Whose voices get heard</h2>

<p>The centering of Israeli perspectives in these earlier works – as well as in “NAZA” – also shows how violence against Palestinians can be given greater credence when it’s described by Israelis themselves. </p>

<p>Recent Palestinian narratives about Gaza, such as “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt32606918/">From Ground Zero</a>” and “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt43743832/">Thirteen in Gaza</a>,” have garnered <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2025/sep/09/from-ground-zero-stories-from-gaza-review-scenes-of-ordinary-life-in-extremis">some attention and praise</a> in <a href="https://deadline.com/2026/09/thirteen-gaza-trailer-father-daughter-palestinian-netpac-1237109243/">the film world</a>, but nowhere near the same amount as “NAZA” has in the weeks since its premiere.</p>

<p>Even “No Other Land,” which is centered on a Palestinian village, features an Israeli journalist and filmmaker, Abraham, documenting the protests and confronting Israeli soldiers, and may not have received the same acclaim if it had been made entirely by Palestinians. </p>

<p>Yet, despite these many barriers, Palestinians have never stopped finding ways to make themselves heard. In addition to films like “Omar” and “200 Meters,” videos and images <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/14781158.2024.2415908">shared directly to social media</a> have allowed Palestinians to connect directly with audiences and shape global awareness of their plight, especially since the current war in Gaza began. </p>

<p>They have been able to bypass the physical barriers that have long restricted their movement – and the cultural barriers that have often kept their experiences out of sight.</p>

<title>Trump has gotten rid of many of the checks and balances that could stop him from demolishing the Kennedy Center</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762129/original/file-20260924-50-s3fk78.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C6000%2C4000&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Musicians perform during a rally against the closing of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts on Sept. 18, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Trump%20Kennedy%20Center/d0e3631e03724912b6556e5ffb0b4d5c/photo">AP Photo/Jose Luis Magana</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Who gets to decide the future of the <a href="https://www.kennedy-center.org/memorial/">living memorial to former President John F. Kennedy</a>, and who holds those decision-makers to account?</p>

<p>This debate is becoming ever more fraught. A <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/17/us/politics/trump-kennedy-center-photos.html">photo taken on Sept. 16, 2026</a>, showed President Donald J. Trump in Air Force One reviewing a poster with the words “Kennedy Center DEMOLISH …” that many interpreted to mean “demolished.”</p>

<p>The image spread quickly. Like the protests that brought <a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/protesters-plan-form-human-chain-kennedy-center-amid/story?id=136558872">throngs of arts lovers to the center a few days later</a>, it amplified the drama around the fate of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C. For more than a half-century, the multivenue complex has featured world-class symphonies, operas, dance and theater performances, along with education programs. </p>

<p>Whether it would be <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/17/arts/music/kennedy-center-closure-emergency-hearing.html">open or closed</a> to the public, active or dormant, repaired or dismantled, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/13/arts/design/trump-kennedy-center-bankruptcy-closure.html">solvent or bankrupt</a> and if it can <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/09/15/trump-kennedy-center-judge/a43ae64a-b123-11f1-92c2-5c918f4a6127_story.html">include Trump’s name in its branding</a> have been the subjects of widespread dispute and speculation since Trump returned to office.</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://www.american.edu/cas/faculty/eataylor.cfm">professor and scholar of arts management</a>, I can explain why the official answers to who gets to decide and who is supposed to hold those deciders accountable are reasonably clear.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
