<h2>Oversight hierarchy collapsed</h2>

<p>Congress <a href="https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?hl=false&amp;edition=2023&amp;req=granuleid%3AUSC-2018-title20-chapter3-subchapter5&amp;num=0">created the Kennedy Center and determines its governance</a>. It’s up to lawmakers, through their power of the purse, to decide on funding for construction, repairs and a portion of its operational budget.</p>

<p>The oversight of facilities and programs falls to a board of trustees that’s authorized by Congress to advance the mission and secure the majority of the center’s earned and contributed revenue. And those operations are, in turn, subject to review by the Internal Revenue Service, which determines the center’s nonprofit status, and federal courts, which determine its compliance with the law.</p>

<p>So how did that hierarchy of oversight essentially collapse into <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/siladityaray/2026/09/16/democrat-says-trump-threw-tantrum-during-kennedy-center-board-meeting-after-court-ruling/">a shouting match between Trump and Rep. Joyce Beatty</a>, an Ohio Democrat, and result in two ongoing lawsuits in U.S. District Court?</p>

<p>Beatty <a href="https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/district-of-columbia/dcdce/1:2025cv04480/287972/50/">filed one of the suits</a> and <a href="https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/72528661/dc-preservation-league-v-board-of-trustees-of-the-john-f-kennedy-center/">a consortium of architects and preservationists</a> filed the other. <a href="https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/judge-kennedy-center-case-orders-trump-administration-explain-closure-plans-2026-09-16/">The same judge</a>, Christopher R. Cooper, is presiding over both cases.</p>



<h2>Presidential control</h2>

<p>The main cause of what I would call a governance failure is that most of those official oversight authorities now serve at the pleasure of the president.</p>

<p>In 2025, the Republican-controlled Congress <a href="https://www.ibtimes.co.uk/kennedy-center-faces-257-million-renovation-what-one-big-beautiful-bill-really-covers-1775497">approved US$257 million</a> for “necessary expenses for capital repair, restoration, maintenance backlog, and security structures” at the Kennedy Center. But most GOP legislators have remained silent about its oversight, including multiple attempts to affix Trump’s name to the building – which <a href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2026/09/15/judge-blocks-kennedy-center-trump-name-inscription-sign/91775374007/">Judge Cooper keeps insisting</a> is something only Congress can allow. </p>

<p>Trump has chaired its board of trustees and appointed the vast majority of its members since <a href="https://theconversation.com/trump-has-purged-the-kennedy-centers-board-which-in-turn-made-him-its-chair-why-does-that-matter-249934">an unprecedented restructuring to the previously bipartisan board</a> in February 2025.</p>

<p>In his <a href="https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/district-of-columbia/dcdce/1:2025cv04480/287972/50/">May 2026 ruling</a>, Judge Cooper found the board of trustees to be “derelict in discharging the full range of its responsibilities to the Center.” More recently, the DC Preservation League has suggested <a href="https://dcpreservation.org/2026/09/17/plaintiffs-call-for-independent-protection-of-the-kennedy-center/">removal of the trustees and appointment of a receiver</a> if current leadership “is unwilling or unable to exercise its fiduciary duty.”</p>

<h2>Agencies aren’t responding</h2>

<p>With both Congress and the trustees aligned with Trump, there are several federal agencies that could be stepping in to critique the board or its decisions: the Internal Revenue Service, the Justice Department, the Office of Management and Budget and others.</p>

<p>But they are all cooperating with the White House in a dramatic consolidation of power by the executive branch that <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/06/29/nx-s1-5816232/supreme-court-ftc-independent-agencies-humphreys-executor">now reaches into traditionally independent federal agencies</a>.</p>

<p>That leaves the federal courts, where Beatty is among the few with standing to sue. She is an <a href="https://www.wsj.com/opinion/stolen-glory-at-the-kennedy-center-121a327f">ex officio member of the board</a>, meaning that she serves by virtue of her role in Congress. She also is willing to stand up and challenge the Trump administration’s attempt to direct – and perhaps even demolish – the Kennedy Center.</p>

<p>Even as these and other construction-related lawsuits are pending, the Trump administration has proven its willingness and ability to build, renovate or destroy federal landmarks without clear authority to do so.</p>

<p>Trump had the White House <a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/new-images-show-entire-white-house-east-wing/story?id=126800684">East Wing demolished</a> in October 2025 without getting Congress to sign off or sharing those plans in advance. And he has <a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/trump-shows-off-multimillion-dollar-white-house-helipad/story?id=135782264">built a new helipad</a> on White House grounds, to name two examples.</p>

<p>Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts has called Trump’s attempt to build a ballroom where the East Wing used to stand without congressional authorization “<a href="https://thehill.com/regulation/court-battles/6062155-roberts-white-house-ballroom-dissent/">likely unlawful</a>.” And yet, construction continues.</p>

<h2>Who decides?</h2>

<p>The buildings on the Kennedy Center campus are only part of what’s at stake.</p>

<p>The Kennedy Center was established as a “living memorial” to former President John F. Kennedy. The “memorial” part is largely associated with the physical campus and its many engravings and artworks honoring Kennedy.</p>

<p>But the “living” component manifests in its live performances, original productions, educational programming, artistic leadership and what audiences, educators and students experience both within and beyond the campus walls.</p>

<p>There were early indicators that both programs and public engagement were faltering under the board’s new leadership. Revenue from performances <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/entertainment/2025/12/07/trump-kennedy-center">began a steep decline</a> after Trump’s takeover in February 2025, well before he announced his intention to <a href="https://theconversation.com/trump-wants-to-shutter-the-kennedy-center-for-2-years-an-arts-management-professor-explains-what-that-portends-274906">close the center for major repairs</a>. It wasn’t just audiences turning away – many artists also <a href="https://www.newsweek.com/entertainment/full-list-acts-pulled-out-trump-changed-kennedy-center-name-11451229">canceled their engagements</a> or stopped making customary bookings.</p>

<p>Prior to that takeover, The Washington Post has reported, the center’s finances had <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/style/2026/08/25/kennedy-center-revenue-plunged-after-trumps-name-went-building/">become increasingly strong</a> as it <a href="https://www.kennedy-center.org/globalassets/our-story/mission/kennedy-center-fy24-budget-justification-to-congress.pdf">recovered from the disruptions</a> that all arts venues suffered during the COVID-19 pandemic. </p>

<p>So, who gets to decide the future of this living memorial to a <a href="https://www.aarp.org/events-history/why-we-love-john-f-kennedy">revered slain president</a>? In the short term, it’s the center’s board, chaired by Trump. And who holds those decision-makers to account? Ongoing federal court cases have constrained or delayed some of those choices. But most other official checks and balances are currently neutral or skewed in the president’s favor. </p>

<p>Public attention through independent journalism and <a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/protesters-plan-form-human-chain-kennedy-center-amid/story?id=136558872">citizen activism</a> can increase friction and shape the political calculus surrounding the Kennedy Center. But any long-term solution will depend on the physical condition of its campus, its adherence to its original mission as a living memorial and the reliable, responsible and accountable governance of its leaders.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292436/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Trump frames unregulated AI as a way to keep ahead of China – but in fact, it harms US national security</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762150/original/file-20260924-50-b3v7d2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C7548%2C5032&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Are Presidents Trump and Xi walking down a dangerous path on AI?</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/president-donald-trump-walks-with-chinas-president-xi-news-photo/2296275067?adppopup=true">Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Amid the chorus of voices calling for <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/12/anthropic-ceo-dario-amodei-seeks-immediate-slowdown-artificial-intelligence-01073519">a slowdown in AI advancement</a> and <a href="https://abcnews.com/US/23-states-urge-congress-regulate-ai-warn-risks/story?id=136711204">more government regulation</a> and oversight of the technology, one prominent contrarian voice stands out: that of Donald J. Trump.</p>

<p>The U.S president has repeatedly argued that the introduction of robust regulations to slow down progress on AI <a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/6089123-trump-resists-ai-regulation-warnings/">threatens U.S. national interests</a> by enabling China to seize the advantage.</p>

<p>“Whoever wins AI, WINS!” Trump <a href="http://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117269745153543631">posted on social media</a> on Sept. 21, 2026, and singled out China as the primary threat to America “winning” AI. He followed up with a speech at the United Nations in which he <a href="https://thehill.com/newsletters/6104340-report/6104340-trump-tells-un-that-ai-needs-a-rebrand/amp/">outlined his administration’s total rejection</a> of “any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control” artificial intelligence.</p>

<p>Certainly, China seizing the global lead on AI would represent an alarming setback to American strategic and economic interests. As a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=dMo5aFUAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">scholar whose research examines the intersection</a> of international relations and technology, I contend that China’s swift advances in AI constitute one of the leading reasons why regulation of the U.S. AI industry is necessary. Paradoxical as it may sound, slowing down AI advancement in the U.S. would also decelerate China’s advances. </p>

<p>Even more important, recent <a href="https://theconversation.com/government-hacks-rogue-agents-and-no-transparency-can-we-ever-fully-trust-ai-292536">revelations about AI “going rogue,”</a> coupled with the astonishing <a href="https://fortune.com/2026/02/24/anthropic-china-deepseek-theft-claude-distillation-copyright-national-security/">growth in power and capability of new AI models</a>, strongly suggest that an unregulated sector represents a greater security threat for the United States than the threat of a surge in capabilities by China.  </p>

<h2>Unregulated AI and security threats</h2>

<p><a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/12/technology/anthropic-dario-amodei-ai-slowdown.html">Leading industry</a> and <a href="https://www.un.org/unispal/document/sg-address-unga-81-22sep26/">political figures</a> around the globe have sounded the alarm about the security threats presented by unchecked AI growth. About 8 in 10 <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/24/politics/cnn-poll-ai-data-centers-vis">Americans share these concerns</a>, according to recent polling, as a large majority of Democrats, Independents and Republicans support increasing AI regulations.</p>

<p>These threats include heightened U.S. vulnerability to attacks from foreign nations and <a href="https://unicri.org/News/Algorithms-Terrorism-UNICRI-UNOCCT">terrorist groups who can exploit AI advances</a> to build <a href="https://hms.harvard.edu/news/risks-artificial-intelligence-weapons-design">more lethal weapons systems</a> – both conventional arms and weapons of mass destruction. Advances in the sector also increase the chance of nefarious actors launching devastating cyberattacks, with <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/five-eyes-intelligence-alliance-warns-that-new-ai-models-pose-urgent-cyber-risk-2026-06-22/?utm_source=chatgpt.com">AI becoming increasingly adept</a> at identifying and exploiting cybersecurity vulnerabilities.</p>

<p>These concerns are known within the industry. On Sept. 10, 2026, Anthropic <a href="http://bbc.com/news/articles/cx2zrrpkx20o?accountMarketingPreferences=off">issued a report</a> revealing a series of incidents in which foreign actors – some based in China, Russia and Iran – used Claude in cyber, influence, surveillance and fraud operations and to support weapons development. Google similarly detected recent attempts by actors linked to China, Russia, North Korea and Iran to <a href="https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/from-prompting-to-autonomy-the-evolution-of-adversarial-ai">use its Gemini AI model</a> to carry out hacking, disinformation, espionage and criminal operations.</p>

<p>Anthropic’s <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/threat-intelligence-report-september-2026">report revealed</a> “five case studies of actors using our models in ways that could support biological weapons development.” </p>

<p>Unregulated AI poses not just a severe security challenge but a <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-would-ai-actually-kill-all-humans-here-are-the-top-5-scenarios-292220">potentially existential threat</a>. An AI-induced nuclear missile launch, the release of super pathogens that cause pandemics and attacks on critical life-sustaining infrastructure have all been raised as potential concerns. Aside from these more extreme scenarios, unchecked AI poses a threat to the digital infrastructure that undergirds the U.S. and world economies.</p>

<h2>Slowing the speedboat</h2>

<p><a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cw980n0nd0qjo">Trump may dismiss these worst-case scenarios</a> as a “hoax,” but the national security threats are real. Trump’s argument is that the best way to protect the U.S. is to make sure American companies stay ahead of China on AI. Indeed, China’s AI models are not far behind, and China possesses an advantage in a factor vital to AI systems – <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/23/us/politics/ai-us-china-trump-xi-economy.html">electric power generation</a>, which AI consumes in large and growing quantities. </p>

<p>Still, the consensus of tech experts is that the U.S. remains the world’s top AI power due to American firms’ lead in <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/23/us/politics/ai-us-china-trump-xi-economy.html">advanced models and computer chips</a> and the scale of America’s computing power – through chips, processors and servers – as well as <a href="https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report">the level of capital investment</a>.  </p>

<p>However, the rapid advance of AI capabilities by American firms has helped China to accelerate its own AI industry.</p>

<p>China <a href="https://fortune.com/2026/02/24/anthropic-china-deepseek-theft-claude-distillation-copyright-national-security/">uses a process known as distillation</a> to exploit cutting-edge U.S. AI models to train China’s own models. The process enables China to develop models nearly as powerful but much more efficient, using far fewer resources.</p>

<p>Beijing’s reliance on distillation, according to <a href="https://carnegieendowment.org/people/matt-sheehan">Matt Sheehan</a>, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, is a result of its own limited computing power, estimated at just one-tenth that of the United States. As a result of its distillation strategy, the pace of <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/15/opinion/ezra-klein-podcast-matt-sheehan.html?smid=nytcore-ios-share">China’s AI progress is tightly linked to U.S. progress</a>. Using Sheenan’s analogy, the relationship is much like a speedboat pulling a water skier: If the U.S. eases on the AI throttle, China will be forced to slow down as well.</p>

<p>Therefore, racing ahead unchecked at breakneck speed – the approach advocated by Trump – would not guarantee that the U.S. widens its AI lead. Chinese firms will continue to exploit U.S. AI progress to <a href="https://thediplomat.com/2026/08/chinas-military-is-now-using-ai-to-plan-strike-operations/">strengthen their offensive capabilities</a>.</p>

<h2>Global governance and regulation</h2>

<p>As such, rather than jeopardizing American national security, U.S. regulations that slow AI advancement could strengthen security by slowing down the Chinese government’s own access to cutting-edge AI.</p>

<p>The “China threat” argument against greater U.S. regulation on AI is also predicated on the notion that Beijing does not possess its own concerns about the dangers of unchecked growth in AI power, and this isn’t the case. </p>

<p>Chinese leaders harbor serious security and domestic affairs–related <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/14/world/asia/china-ai-security-risks-anthropic.html">concerns about uncontrolled AI growth</a>. Indeed, if there is one AI area where China leads the U.S., it is in regulations on AI. Consider, for example, that as far back as 2021, Beijing imposed its <a href="https://carnegieendowment.org/research/2024/02/tracing-the-roots-of-chinas-ai-regulations?utm_source=chatgpt.com">first major set of AI regulations</a>.</p>

<p>And while top figures in the Trump administration were urging less regulation, Chinese officials were calling for the opposite. In recent months, Chinese officials have repeatedly called for greater <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/09/25/trump-rejects-demands-ai-rules-while-xi-calls-human-control/">domestic and international oversight of AI</a>. China’s leader, Xi Jinping, has been enthusiastic about AI advances, but his speech at the 2026 World AI Conference in Shanghai urgently <a href="https://www.ft.com/content/ddb316b4-c6ae-4b9b-9d4a-63d63201d4fc?utm_source=chatgpt.com&amp;syn-25a6b1a6=1">expressed the need for strong AI regulations and oversight</a>.</p>

<p>Speaking at the U.N. Security Council’s meeting on AI and International Security on Sept. 23, 2026, Fu Cong, China’s permanent representative to the United Nations, <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/23/us-chinese-visions-for-ai-regulation-differ-sharply-at-un-meeting-01090906">made the case for</a> “a consensus-based global governance framework” for AI to “build institutional guardrails that preserve international peace and security.”</p>

<p>Beijing appears to be framing unregulated AI advancement not as a race but as a common threat. Should Trump be convinced by such a narrative, then there may be grounds for optimism that Washington and Beijing in the near future will be able to reach agreement on AI governance and regulation – a development that would better ensure a safer future for both nations.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292642/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Gen Z communicates differently in the workplace, but older colleagues can still decode them</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762017/original/file-20260924-72-xnnd8i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5184%2C3456&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Young workers often share values with older colleagues, but the environment where they learned about workplace behavior is different.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://unsplash.com/photos/a-man-sitting-in-front-of-a-laptop-computer-7nQGQ0ve5A0">Sebastian Herrmann on Unsplash</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>For all the talk about <a href="https://theconversation.com/young-professionals-are-struggling-to-socially-adapt-in-the-workplace-educators-can-help-237845">generational differences</a> at work, some of the biggest differences show up in surprisingly ordinary moments.</p>

<p>Take being late for work. A <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2019/01/17/where-millennials-end-and-generation-z-begins/">Gen Z</a> employee in her 20s I spoke with works at a small, locally owned café and restaurant run by an older Gen X owner. When she realized she was going to be late one day, she texted him. He was frustrated. To him, being late was serious enough to warrant a phone call, and a text felt too casual and impersonal. </p>

<p>She saw the exact same interaction very differently. </p>

<p>“He’s super busy, so I felt a call was going to take up too much time,” she told me. “So I texted. I thought it was more considerate.” </p>

<p>Both thought they understood what respectful workplace communication looked like. They just had completely different definitions of it.</p>

<p><a href="https://jeffleblancdba.com/">I study workplace culture</a> and communication, and I see this type of misunderstanding as increasingly common in multigenerational workplaces. And this is becoming more pronounced as Gen Z moves further into the workforce. The <a href="https://www.fastcompany.com/91369085/ready-or-not-gen-z-is-managing-you-gen-z-work-management">oldest members of Gen Z</a> are now approaching 30, while the youngest are in college and high school.</p>

<p>What’s distinctive about the older members of Gen Z is that many went through college, internships or their first jobs <a href="https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0249792&amp;utm">during the COVID-19 pandemic</a>, when much of our communication moved online and masks often covered half our faces. And there’s a new twist now, as artificial intelligence changes how we communicate all over again. </p>

<p>The result isn’t necessarily that Gen Z employees communicate better or worse with their bosses and colleagues than previous generations did. I argue that they have simply learned to do so in a very different environment.</p>

<h2>When a text means something more</h2>

<p>The café example is an easy one to dismiss as younger workers <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/08934215.2025.2542562">preferring texting</a> and feeling that phone calls are for important occasions only. </p>

<p>But that misses what I think is the more interesting point: The employee wasn’t trying to avoid her boss. She thought she was respecting his time. </p>

<p>For her boss, by contrast, the phone call itself carried meaning. It communicated that she understood the seriousness of being late. </p>

<p>Neither one had explained that expectation to the other.</p>

<p>Managers shouldn’t assume employees attach the same meaning they do to a particular form of communication. If being late requires a phone call, they need to say so. A two-minute conversation about expectations can prevent both people from walking away from an interaction believing the other was disrespectful.</p>

<p>Another common stumble concerns openness, which might feel like oversharing.</p>

<p>One Gen Z worker I spoke with had recently started a job at a large New England company in a blue-collar industry. He was struggling with severe anxiety and decided to tell his <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/social-trends/2008/06/25/baby-boomers-the-gloomiest-generation/">baby boomer</a> manager. The manager was sympathetic, but also uneasy. </p>

<p>“It made me feel uncomfortable, if I’m being honest,” the manager told me. “I didn’t want to downplay his anxiety, but I’m not sure I needed to know.”</p>

<p>That distinction matters. His reaction wasn’t that anxiety wasn’t real or that his employee should simply get over it. But he questioned how much of it belonged in their professional relationship. </p>

<p>Many older workers learned that professionalism is about setting clear boundaries between personal and professional life. Members of Gen Z are coming of age during a period when conversations about <a href="https://hbr.org/2019/10/research-people-want-their-employers-to-talk-about-mental-health">mental health</a> and personal well-being are considerably more public. What feels like honesty to one person can feel like oversharing to their boss. </p>

<p>This doesn’t mean that managers have to become therapists, and employees don’t have to disclose everything happening in their lives. But both may need to recognize that their comfort level around disclosure isn’t universal.</p>

              <span class="caption">What younger workers may see as honesty could be seen as oversharing by older colleagues, who tend to keep more boundaries over personal information.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://unsplash.com/photos/woman-in-gray-sweater-using-silver-macbook-r_-zzXrnzxI">Aleksandra Sapozhnikova on Unsplash</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Learning to read a room when the room disappeared</h2>

<p>Some workplace communication is never spoken at all. Think about how people traditionally learned to read a room. They watched faces around a conference table. They noticed a change in a manager’s tone. Someone caught them after a meeting and quietly explained what had just happened. </p>

<p>Now think about someone who was 18 or 19 in 2020.</p>

<p>At exactly the age when many young people would have been developing these skills in college, internships and early jobs, the room disappeared. Classes went online. Internships became remote. When people returned in person, masks sometimes made facial communication more difficult. </p>

<p>That doesn’t mean members of Gen Z can’t read facial expressions, but we should be careful about assuming everyone had the same opportunities to learn the unwritten signals of professional life. If feedback matters, I believe managers should say it. A disappointed expression on a Zoom call is a poor substitute for a conversation.</p>

<h2>I thought that was understood</h2>

<p>Imagine a manager telling a young employee: “I need this by Friday.” The employee sends it back at 4:30 p.m. that Friday afternoon. The manager is annoyed because they intended to review it that morning, make changes and send it along to someone else. </p>

<p>The employee is equally confused. The deadline was Friday, and they met it.</p>

<p>This deadline mismatch gets at something I have repeatedly encountered in my research with Gen Z workers. <a href="https://al-kindipublisher.com/index.php/jbms/article/view/12577">In a survey</a> I conducted of 250 Gen Z professionals across industries, clear structural expectations emerged alongside fairness and empathetic engagement as recurring themes.</p>

<p>If an <a href="https://www.fastcompany.com/91281732/gen-z-isnt-quiet-quitting-theyre-rejecting-outdated-leadership">employee wants clarity</a>, it shouldn’t automatically be confused with hand-holding. An employee can want autonomy and still want to know exactly what success looks like. “Friday” and “Friday by 10 a.m. because I need three hours to review this” communicate very different expectations.</p>

<p>Artificial intelligence may make this issue even more important. We can now produce polished emails, summarize meetings and generate information faster than ever. But more communication does not guarantee more understanding.</p>

<p>I believe that may be the larger lesson for every generation working together. We tend to mistake the workplace norms we learned for common sense. They aren’t. They were taught to us by the workplaces, technologies and moments in history in which we began our careers.</p>

<p>Gen Z is learning theirs in a very different world.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292108/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: Young workers often share values with older colleagues, but the environment where they learned about workplace behavior is different
Sebastian Herrmann on Unsplash , CC BY For all the talk about generational differences at work, some of the biggest differences show up in surprisingly ordinary moments
A Gen Z employee in her 20s I spoke with works at a small, locally owned café and restaurant run by an older Gen X owner
When she realized she was going to be late one day, she texted him
To him, being late was serious enough to warrant a phone call, and a text felt too casual and impersonal
She saw the exact same interaction very differently. “He’s super busy, so I felt a call was going to take up too much time,” she told me. “So I texted
I thought it was more considerate.” Both thought they understood what respectful workplace communication looked like
They just had completely different definitions of it
I study workplace culture and communication, and I see this type of misunderstanding as increasingly common in multigenerational workplaces
And this is becoming more pronounced as Gen Z moves further into the workforce
The oldest members of Gen Z are now approaching 30, while the youngest are in college and high school

What’s distinctive about the older members of Gen Z is that many went through college, internships or their first jobs during the COVID-19 pandemic , when much of our communication moved online and masks often covered half our faces
And there’s a new twist now, as artificial intelligence changes how we communicate all over again
The result isn’t necessarily that Gen Z employees communicate better or worse with their bosses and colleagues than previous generations did
I argue that they have simply learned to do so in a very different environment
When a text means something more The café example is an easy one to dismiss as younger workers preferring texting and feeling that phone calls are for important occasions only
But that misses what I think is the more interesting point: The employee wasn’t trying to avoid her boss
For her boss, by contrast, the phone call itself carried meaning
It communicated that she understood the seriousness of being late
Neither one had explained that expectation to the other
Managers shouldn’t assume employees attach the same meaning they do to a particular form of communication
If being late requires a phone call, they need to say so
A two-minute conversation about expectations can prevent both people from walking away from an interaction believing the other was disrespectful
Another common stumble concerns openness, which might feel like oversharing
One Gen Z worker I spoke with had recently started a job at a large New England company in a blue-collar industry
He was struggling with severe anxiety and decided to tell his baby boomer manager

The manager was sympathetic, but also uneasy. “It made me feel uncomfortable, if I’m being honest,” the manager told me. “I didn’t want to downplay his anxiety, but I’m not sure I needed to know.” That distinction matters
His reaction wasn’t that anxiety wasn’t real or that his employee should simply get over it
But he questioned how much of it belonged in their professional relationship
Many older workers learned that professionalism is about setting clear boundaries between personal and professional life
Members of Gen Z are coming of age during a period when conversations about mental health and personal well-being are considerably more public
What feels like honesty to one person can feel like oversharing to their boss
This doesn’t mean that managers have to become therapists, and employees don’t have to disclose everything happening in their lives
But both may need to recognize that their comfort level around disclosure isn’t universal
What younger workers may see as honesty could be seen as oversharing by older colleagues, who tend to keep more boundaries over personal information
Aleksandra Sapozhnikova on Unsplash , CC BY Learning to read a room when the room disappeared Some workplace communication is never spoken at all
Think about how people traditionally learned to read a room
They watched faces around a conference table
They noticed a change in a manager’s tone
Someone caught them after a meeting and quietly explained what had just happened

David Ake/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Felicita Piñón weighed just 1 pound at birth. She was later diagnosed with cerebral palsy that requires her to use a power wheelchair, and she also has learning and emotional challenges. Yet despite these obstacles, Felicita, now an eighth grade student, is just like any other happy, active teenager who hasn’t let her disability limit her. She also did something remarkable that’s not typical of most teens – in 2025, she testified against a school voucher bill at the Texas Capitol. </p>

<p>But in 2024, when Felicita wanted to join a cheerleading team at her Crowley, Texas, middle school, her mother, Liz Piñón, said the school was not willing to make accommodations for her, as she felt <a href="https://www.ed.gov/laws-and-policy/individuals-disabilities">federal disabilities laws</a> required. She believed the school was discriminating against her daughter on the basis of her disability, as well as her race. She also noted that she knew of other nearby schools that had girls in wheelchairs who participated on cheerleading teams. </p>

<p>As a result, Piñón – <a href="https://www.ed.gov/media/document/ocr-report-president-and-secretary-of-education-2024-109012.pdf">like thousands of others that year</a> – filed a complaint with the federal Education Department’s <a href="https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-offices/ocr">Office for Civil Rights</a>. </p>

<p>For decades, the Office for Civil Rights, or OCR, served as a critical safety net when local schools <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/06/16/nx-s1-5717030/special-ed-civil-rights-education-department">failed to meet federal</a> disability standards. Now, <a href="https://www.edweek.org/policy-politics/special-ed-and-civil-rights-what-we-know-about-the-ed-dept-s-latest-moves/2026/06">sweeping budget and workforce cuts</a> have restructured the office, leading to the <a href="https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-26-108320">dismissal of thousands of complaints</a> without investigation and raising urgent questions about who will enforce federal special education laws when states fall short. </p>

<p>And while large caseloads, according to disability rights advocates, are not new for the Office for Civil Rights, parents at least used to receive confirmation that their complaint was received and being looked at. Today, however, it is not uncommon for parents to not receive confirmation – or any follow-ups to their case – even after it’s been dismissed. </p>

<p>Piñón’s <a href="https://docs.google.com/document/d/1amPaTzSttVj992KB8IbAMeu8KupW8II3I4EKVHCSvNc/edit?tab=t.0">complaint was rejected in July 2024</a>, denied access to this link before President Donald Trump took office and ushered in the cuts at the Department of Education. It wasn’t the outcome she wanted, but it did provide her with important information and closure, and gave her comfort that she had a place to turn.</p>

<p>“Even though the department wasn’t perfect,” Piñón told me, “they still provided an extra layer of rights, guidance and technical assistance for schools and districts.”  </p>

<p><a href="https://education.utexas.edu/faculty/david_dematthews/">As a teacher</a> and district administrator in West Baltimore and in Washington, I’ve seen firsthand how difficult it can be for states, districts and schools to implement special education law on their own. And now as a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=ekLOu04AAAAJ&amp;hl=en">professor and researcher</a> at the University of Texas, I focus much of my work on improving schools for students with disabilities. I have talked to parents, advocates and school officials, many of whom are greatly concerned that cuts to the OCR will be harmful.</p>

<p>For parents like Piñón, the question now is not whether the system has ever worked perfectly, but whether families can continue to look to the Education Department and the Office for Civil Rights for support when states, districts and schools fail to meet their obligations in giving all children a quality education.</p>

<h2>An office designed for equity</h2>

<p>Since its creation in 1980, the relatively small Department of Education Office for Civil Rights has had a large task: enforcing federal civil rights laws that prohibit discrimination in schools based on race, color, national origin, sex, disability and age. </p>

<p>Parents often work first with their child’s teachers and principals to resolve disagreements over whether a child with disabilities is receiving adequate support in school. If parents want to escalate a complaint they feel was not dealt with, they may also reach out to district superintendents and even state officials. </p>

<p>Filing a civil rights complaint with the Office for Civil Rights can be parents’ last stop. This office was typically their only free direct line to connect with the Education Department. </p>

<p><iframe id="yRLXk" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/yRLXk/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Line graph that displays the rise in OCR complaints over time."></iframe></p>

<p>I have seen firsthand that parents know contacting OCR can be a slow, and sometimes frustrating, process. Yet it remained an important avenue through which parents felt their concerns could be heard and elevated to a higher level.  </p>

<h2>Radio silence from OCR</h2>

<p>In March 2025, the Education Department cut nearly half of the entire agency’s <a href="https://www.highereddive.com/news/ed-dept-staff-changes-statutory-responsibilities-OIG-RIF/823590/">nearly 4,000-person workforce</a>. </p>

<p>This included an estimated 299 out of 575 staff positions at the OCR, <a href="https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-26-108320">according to the Government Accountability Office</a>. </p>

<p>After litigation challenging the cuts, <a href="https://www.edweek.org/policy-politics/ed-dept-hasnt-complied-with-order-to-restore-civil-rights-staff-judge-says/2025/08">some employees at the Office for Civil Rights have been reinstated</a>. The Education Department subsequently reported in November 2025 that there were 446 staff members at the OCR, including 384 who had initially received termination notices. </p>

<p>Even though the office retained over 75% of its pre-Trump staff, people who submitted complaints received new point people responsible for their cases, and in some cases did not receive follow-up. </p>

<p>In addition, <a href="https://www.edweek.org/policy-politics/ed-dept-paid-civil-rights-staffers-up-to-38-million-as-it-tried-to-lay-them-off/2026/02">seven out of 12 regional OCR branches</a> permanently closed around this time: Atlanta, Boston, Cleveland, Chicago, Dallas, Philadelphia and San Francisco.</p>

<p>Education Secretary Linda McMahon described the cuts and shifts at the department in April 2026 as <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/04/28/nx-s1-5802968/education-secretary-linda-mcmahon-senate-hearing">necessary to increase “accountability” and “efficiency.”</a> </p>

<p>Then, in June, the <a href="https://www.ed.gov/media/document/fact-sheet-department-of-education-and-department-of-health-and-human-services-special-education-and-rehabilitative-services-partnership-114238.pdf">Education Department announced</a> that the Department of Justice would take a larger role in civil rights investigations. </p>

<p>While the exact nature of these changes for students is not clear, the announcement is amplifying some advocates and families’ concern about whether an agency with limited education experience can effectively safeguard the rights of students with disabilities.</p>

<p>From the date of the initial cuts in March through September 2025, the Office for Civil Rights <a href="https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-26-108320">received over 9,000 new complaints</a> of alleged discrimination and reported as resolved over 7,000 of those complaints during that time frame. About 90% of those complaints categorized as resolved were actually dismissed by the Education Department, the GAO found.</p>

<p>Advocates say parents are not getting responses from the department. </p>

<p>“We are hearing from parents it is radio silence from OCR. They are just waiting to hear anything, and they are not feeling like they are getting any feedback or being asked any details or questions,” said Robyn Linscott, director of education and family policy at the disability advocacy nonprofit <a href="https://www.thearcoftexas.org/">The Arc of Texas</a>, which advocates for Texans with intellectual and developmental disabilities and their families. </p>

<p>In some cases, filed complaints are marked as resolved “when they were never really investigated. No one went to the school and called them, or asked any questions,” Linscott told The Conversation.</p>

<p>Meanwhile, parents who filed complaints and did not hear back, or had their cases dismissed, are “out of options or have to try to resolve their issue with the state or hire an attorney, if they have the means to do that,” according to Denise Marshall, the CEO at Council of Parent Attorneys and Advocates, a national disability rights nonprofit.</p>

<p>The education legal team at <a href="https://disabilityrightstx.org/en/category/community-living/?gad_source=1&amp;gad_campaignid=20947440363&amp;gbraid=0AAAAACF1BgZ477bkdxtKn-hnSSy_vSBY-&amp;gclid=Cj0KCQjwzY7VBhDwARIsAFtPvBRs9TIWskWs7oEuht5LUp7BiNe92wyklr0DcemRsFYSchQHBIjEhWgaAuRAEALw_wcB">Disability Rights Texas</a>, a nonprofit legal and advocacy organization that advocates for the legal rights of Texans with disabilities, also has seen harmful changes. This organization helps parents through the process, including helping them file complaints with the OCR. </p>

<p>In Texas, after the Dallas Office for Civil Rights office shut its doors, Disability Rights Texas “stopped getting acknowledgments that the office received the complaints,” Colleen Potts, a supervising attorney with the organization, told The Conversation.</p>

<p>“We didn’t know where complaints were going, though OCR was still accepting them,” Potts said.</p>

<p>She directed her team’s attorneys “not to take up resources and time filing OCR complaints.” </p>

<p>The Office for Civil Rights didn’t respond to a request for comment.</p>

<h2>The case for federal oversight</h2>

<p>More than 50 years ago, Congress anticipated that families and schools would not always agree about what students with disabilities need to receive a meaningful education – or that states, districts, and schools would always implement special education law as intended. </p>

<p>In 1975, Congress passed an act, later named the <a href="https://www.ed.gov/laws-and-policy/individuals-disabilities/individuals-disabilities-education-act-idea">Individuals with Disabilities Education Act</a>, or IDEA, that established rights for students with disabilities, while giving the federal government the responsibility to monitor schools’ and states’ implementation of the law. A few years later, <a href="https://www.ed.gov/laws-and-policy/individuals-disabilities/section-504">Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act</a> also allowed families to file civil rights complaints when they believed a student had been discriminated against. </p>

<p>The Education Department’s Office of Special Education Programs helps oversee those state reviews and provides monitoring, support and enforcement for school districts when problems persist. The Education Department has historically helped states and districts understand new legal requirements, and provided guidance and training on everything from helping schools identify students with disabilities to making sure those students receive appropriate services and accommodations.</p>

<p>Yet it was an imperfect system even before the recent cuts. In 2025, for example, <a href="https://sites.ed.gov/idea/idea-files/2025-determination-letters-on-state-implementation-of-idea/">only 21 states met federal special education requirements</a>. And <a href="https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-106264">many, if not most</a>, students with disabilities attend public schools that do not have a psychologist or social worker needed to help evaluate them.</p>

<p>During the 2023-24 school year, nearly every state reported <a href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/states-face-different-special-education-staffing-challenges-that-require-targeted-responses/">special education teacher shortages</a>. </p>

<p>When schools lack the personnel needed to evaluate students, coordinate services, address academic and behavioral needs and support families, students with disabilities are more likely to fall behind <a href="https://access.heinonline.com/HOL/LandingPage?handle=hein.journals/nylr93&amp;div=33&amp;id=&amp;page=">academically and experience poorer outcomes</a> later in life. </p>

<h2>Failed implementation of disability rights law in Texas</h2>

<p>Trump’s 2025 executive order pledges to “<a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/03/improving-education-outcomes-by-empowering-parents-states-and-communities/">return authority over education to the States and local communities</a>,” a <a href="https://www.heritage.org/education/report/the-shrinking-federal-footprint-education-returns-the-states">goal of many critics</a> of federal oversight.</p>

<p>Yet Texas offers a cautionary reminder of what can happen when federal oversight fails, or is not present. </p>

<p>For years, Texas set a target that <a href="https://epaa.asu.edu/index.php/epaa/article/view/3793/2190">pressured school districts</a> to keep the number of students receiving special education at or below 8.5%.</p>

<p>Following a federal investigation, the Office of Special Education Programs <a href="https://specialeducationaction.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/1.11.18-Texas-DMS-letter.pdf">concluded in 2018 that Texas had failed</a> to ensure that students eligible for special needs services were properly “identified, located, and evaluated” and that all children with disabilities received a free appropriate public education. </p>

<p>The Education Department placed Texas on a five-year corrective action plan in 2018, requiring the state to strengthen compliance with IDEA.</p>

<p>Yet even after federal intervention and the corrective action plan, large districts like Houston and Austin school districts struggled to <a href="https://interactive.khou.com/pdfs/Houstonz_ISD_INV2018-08-031_ER2019-01-002_FINAL_Report_9292020.pdf">meet IDEA requirements for thousands of children over several years</a>. </p>

<p>In 2025, <a href="https://sites.ed.gov/idea/spp-apr-letters?selected-category=sppapr-part-b&amp;selected-year=&amp;state=Texas">Texas met IDEA requirements</a> for the first time in years. This followed years of federal monitoring and corrective action. Federal oversight did not eliminate every problem, but it pushed the state to identify systemic failures and created pressure for change. </p>

<p>“We are missing that heavy-handed, federal oversight to come in and say, ‘You messed up and here is how we are ordering you to fix it,’” said Potts, the attorney at Disability Rights Texas.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/285208/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761834/original/file-20260923-50-jh9p0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C27%2C1024%2C682&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Many older school buildings lack air conditioning, leaving fans as the main defense against classroom heat.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/fan-moves-air-around-in-a-3rd-grade-classroom-at-corey-news-photo/2177495412?adppopup=true">RJ Sangosti/MediaNews Group/The Denver Post via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>For many southwestern Pennsylvania students, this school year has already included days away from the classroom because of the buildings themselves. <a href="https://www.wtae.com/article/monessen-school-district-delays-start-2026-2027-fungal-growth/73442537">Mold</a> has closed schools in at least four districts, and early September heat pushed <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/pittsburgh/news/pittsburgh-public-schools-remote-learning-extreme-heat/">35 Pittsburgh Public Schools buildings</a> to remote learning.</p>

<p>The problems aren’t limited to the region: A 2025 <a href="https://www.cityandstatepa.com/politics/2025/08/study-pa-schools-plagued-widespread-lead-mold-radon-and-other-environmental-hazards/407569/">statewide study</a> found that environmental hazards, including mold, lead and radon, are widespread in Pennsylvania schools.</p>

<p>The age and upkeep of these school buildings affect students’ health and their ability to learn. Kids spend <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2014/09/02/school-days-how-the-u-s-compares-with-other-countries/">more than 1,000 hours</a> in school each year; students tend to do better in schools with <a href="https://www.epa.gov/iaq-schools/how-does-indoor-air-quality-impact-student-health-and-academic-performance">healthy indoor environments</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=SfyPpq4AAAAJ&amp;hl=en">I’m an epidemiologist</a> who studies how environmental exposures affect health, with a focus on western Pennsylvania. </p>

<h2>Sick old facilities</h2>

<p>Mold caused the most widespread disruptions. <a href="https://www.wtae.com/article/monessen-school-district-delays-start-2026-2027-fungal-growth/73442537">Monessen City School District</a>, <a href="https://www.heraldstandard.com/news/local_news/2026/sep/15/remediation-wraps-up-at-laurel-highlands-middle-school/">Laurel Highlands Middle School</a>, <a href="https://www.latrobebulletinnews.com/news/lvsd-reopens-remaining-two-schools-as-mold-removal-wraps-up/article_8840492c-af68-4591-b712-6019c74dd795.html">Ligonier Valley School District</a> and <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/pittsburgh/news/homer-center-school-district-delays-school-mold/">Homer-Center School District</a> all delayed the start of school this year or canceled in-person classes due to mold in school buildings that needed to be removed. </p>

<p><a href="https://citizenportal.ai/articles/7813444/pennsylvania/school-districts/central-valley-sd/superintendent-outlines-asbestos-abatement-at-high-school-work-to-begin-may-4">Central Valley School District</a> in Beaver County is currently under construction for asbestos abatement in its middle- and high-school buildings – both built in the 1960s. Students are still attending school in both buildings despite the abatement.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/pittsburgh/news/pittsburgh-public-schools-remote-learning-extreme-heat/">Pittsburgh Public Schools</a> also closed all schools in late August, moving to remote learning, because of a heat wave. Buildings either did not have or could not provide adequate cooling to ensure students were in a safe, healthy environment for learning.</p>

<p>The average age of a Pennsylvania school building is <a href="https://womenforahealthyenvironment.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/SOSreport2025.15.pdf">70 years</a>, about <a href="https://womenforahealthyenvironment.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/SOSreport2025.15.pdf">20 years older</a> than the national average. Pittsburgh Public School buildings <a href="https://community.triblive.com/c/bethel-park-journal/news/4102401">average 90 years old</a>.</p>

<h2>Mold and health</h2>

<p><a href="https://www.epa.gov/mold/what-mold">Molds</a> are a type of fungus. They produce tiny single-cell reproductive units called spores, and when they land in damp indoor environments, they can grow and grow and grow. When there is mold in a building, it releases spores, allergens and other irritants that can cause both <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/mold-health/about/index.html">immediate and long-term health effects</a>.</p>

<p>Short-term exposure to mold can cause <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/mold/health-problems/index.html">sinus congestion, coughing, wheezing, eye irritation and skin rashes</a>. Long-term exposure can lead to long-term health consequences, including <a href="https://axonintegrativehealth.com/blogs/the-long-term-health-effects-of-mold-exposure/">chronic bronchitis or asthma, inflammation of the lungs, headaches, memory loss and fatigue</a>. </p>

<p>Remediation of mold is a challenging process – one that requires <a href="https://www.epa.gov/mold/brief-guide-mold-moisture-and-your-home">immediate action</a>, as mold spreads fast and does more damage to property and health the longer it grows. Buildings with mold must clean up or remediate the mold and remove the water or moisture that is the source of the problem, or else the mold will return.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://aafa.org/allergies/types-of-allergies/mold-allergy/">Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America</a> notes that mold can trigger severe asthma attacks in children already suffering from asthma.</p>

<h2>Heat and health</h2>

<p>During a <a href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/state/pennsylvania/pittsburgh/2026/08/31/pittsburgh-major-heat-september-hot-school-storms/91544108007/">September 2026 heat wave</a> in Pennsylvania, outdoor temperatures in the Pittsburgh area reached the 90s. Under its <a href="https://www.pghschools.org/about/delays-and-closures">extreme heat protocol</a>, Pittsburgh Public Schools monitors classroom temperatures during heat waves and considers remote learning when instructional spaces reach 90 degrees or higher.</p>

<p>High indoor temperatures can make students uncomfortable and raise the risk of heat-related illness. The body’s ability to regulate its temperature in extremely hot environments is limited. <a href="https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/climate-change-heat-and-health">Heat exhaustion and heatstroke</a> are two common health effects that occur when an individual is unable to regulate their temperature. </p>

<p>As the body tries to cool itself, it puts strain on both the heart and kidneys. As a result, heat waves can make <a href="https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/climate-change-heat-and-health">chronic conditions worse and cause acute kidney injuries</a>.</p>

<p>Heat also affects learning. A study of <a href="https://www.nber.org/papers/w24639">10 million students</a> who took the PSAT found that each 1 degree Fahrenheit increase in average school-year temperature reduced learning that year by about 1%.</p>

<h2>Other risks in older schools</h2>

<p>Given the age of school buildings in Pennsylvania, many buildings likely contain <a href="https://www.cityandstatepa.com/politics/2025/08/study-pa-schools-plagued-widespread-lead-mold-radon-and-other-environmental-hazards/407569/">lead paint or pipes as well as asbestos and sometimes radon</a>. </p>

<p>Lead is a naturally occurring metal which, when ingested, can cause neurological problems. Lead poisoning can cause <a href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/lead-poisoning/symptoms-causes/syc-20354717">learning disabilities and developmental delays</a>. </p>

<p>Health officials say <a href="https://www.alleghenyfront.org/lead-testing-isnt-required-for-pa-school-water-fountains-lawmakers-want-to-change-that/">no amount of lead is safe for children</a>. In schools, lead can come from deteriorating paint or from old plumbing, where <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/education/programs-and-services/schools/safe-schools/laws-and-regulations/lead-in-drinking-water.html">water that sits unused in pipes can pick up lead</a>. Pennsylvania schools aren’t required to test their water for lead as long as they discuss the issue at an annual public meeting, and a provision in this year’s state budget <a href="https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2026/07/lead-testing-schools-pennsylvania-relax-standards-flawed-law-education/">loosened reporting rules</a> for schools that do test.</p>

<p>Asbestos is a group of fibrous substances that are both <a href="https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/asbestos">fire resistant and carcinogenic</a>. Students could be exposed to asbestos in older buildings if pipes, boilers or ducts are not properly maintained. The <a href="https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2009-title15/html/USCODE-2009-title15-chap53-subchapII.htm">Asbestos Hazard Emergency Response Act</a> requires public school districts to inspect school buildings for asbestos-containing materials and prepare a management plan to prevent and reduce exposure to asbestos. </p>

<p>Radon is a naturally occurring colorless, odorless gas that <a href="https://www.cancer.org/cancer/risk-prevention/radiation-exposure/radon.html">can cause lung cancer</a>. It seeps into older school buildings through <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/radon/about/index.html">cracks in the foundation and open drains</a>. The <a href="https://www.epa.gov/radon/radon-schools">Environmental Protection Agency estimates</a> that nearly 1 in 5 schools has at least one classroom with a short-term radon level above the action level of concern. Schools should <a href="https://www.lung.org/clean-air/indoor-air/indoor-air-pollutants/radon/schools">monitor radon levels regularly and fix</a> any high levels with mitigation systems. </p>

<h2>Growing bodies, greater risks</h2>

<p>“<a href="https://www.rachelcarson.org/silent-spring">Silent Spring</a>,” written by Pittsburgh-area native Rachel Carson, was published 64 years ago this month. </p>

<p>The book describes a spring when birds’ songs cannot be heard because of toxic chemicals in their environment. It documents the environmental impact on human health and the health of the birds. Carson made it ever-so clear that our environment has a significant impact on our health. </p>

<p>One of the basic tenets of environmental toxicology is that <a href="https://peht.ucsf.edu/concept_detail.php?topic=concept1">children are not small adults</a>. This truth was made clear in “<a href="https://theconversation.com/silent-spring-60-years-on-4-essential-reads-on-pesticides-and-the-environment-192232">Silent Spring</a>,” where Carson’s central warning was that chemicals in the environment end up in our bodies. For children, whose bodies are still developing, that exposure can carry greater risks.</p>



<p>The effects of mold are especially hard on the developing airways of children. Children have a higher sensitivity to not just mold spores but also indoor dampness. </p>

<p>Healthy indoor environments are essential for student learning. <a href="https://www.epa.gov/schools">Federal</a> and <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/health/programs/school-health/environmental">state</a> health, environmental and educational departments offer a range of services, educational materials and grants to support schools that want to improve the indoor environments. </p>
